title: Async, promises, the event loop
blurb: The event loop, microtasks, promise combinators, and the five ways async/await quietly goes wrong. Expect at least one of these in every JavaScript interview.

questions.q: What order do these log?
choices: a d b c
a c d b
a d c b
a b c d
questions.why: Synchronous code runs first (a, d). Then the microtask queue drains completely (c), and only then does the event loop take the next task, the timer (b). The tempting `a d b c` assumes a 0 ms timer is due before the promise callback, but a timer is a task and every queued microtask runs before any task.
questions.asked: The definitive event-loop question. Getting the order right matters less than being able to say why.

questions.q: What is the difference between the task queue and the microtask queue?
choices: Microtasks run on a separate thread, so a long chain of them never blocks rendering
The microtask queue drains completely after each task, before the next task or render
The event loop alternates fairly, taking one task and then one microtask each turn
Tasks hold I/O and timer callbacks, while microtasks hold CPU work the engine splits up
questions.why: Promise callbacks and `queueMicrotask` go on the microtask queue, which runs to exhaustion after the current task; `setTimeout`, I/O and events are tasks. There is no fair alternation: a microtask that keeps queueing microtasks starves timers and rendering entirely.
questions.asked: The follow-up is 'so can a promise chain block the UI?', and the answer is yes.

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
choices: `results` stays empty, because `push` runs before each awaited request resolves
A rejected request is skipped and the loop carries on with the next id in the list
Every request fires at once, so the API sees a burst of 100 simultaneous calls
Each request waits for the previous one, so 100 ids means 100 round trips in series
questions.why: The code is correct but serial: each iteration pauses until its request finishes. If the requests are independent, `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchUser))` runs them concurrently. The burst choice describes that `Promise.all` version, not this loop; serial is right only when calls depend on each other or you must limit load.
questions.asked: The most common real async performance bug, and it looks completely reasonable.

questions.q: What does `Promise.all` do when one of its promises rejects?
choices: It waits for every promise, then resolves with an array of values and errors
It rejects with that error at once; the other operations keep running unobserved
It cancels the other pending operations, then rejects with the first error it saw
It drops the failed entry and resolves with the values that did succeed
questions.why: `Promise.all` is fail-fast. Promises have no cancellation, so the other requests still complete; you just never see their results. The array of values and errors is `Promise.allSettled`, and stopping the others needs an `AbortController`.
questions.asked: Then: 'when would you use allSettled instead?' Dashboards where one failed widget should not blank the page.

questions.q: Which combinator resolves with the first promise to FULFIL, ignoring rejections until all fail?
choices: `Promise.race`
`Promise.allSettled`
`Promise.any`
`Promise.all`
questions.why: `any` waits for the first success and only rejects, with an `AggregateError`, if every input rejects. `race` settles on the first promise to settle either way, so a fast rejection wins it.
questions.asked: race vs any is a clean way to check whether someone has actually used these rather than heard of them.

questions.q: What does this log in Node?
choices: Promise { <pending> }
Promise { undefined }
Promise { 1 }
questions.why: An async function always returns a promise wrapping whatever you return. The body runs synchronously to its `return`, so the promise is already fulfilled when logged, not pending. Chrome prints the same thing as `Promise {<fulfilled>: 1}`.
questions.asked: The origin of 'why is my function returning a Promise instead of the data?'

questions.q: In Node 24, what happens by default when a promise rejects and nothing handles it?
choices: Node prints the error and the process exits with a non-zero code
Node logs an UnhandledPromiseRejectionWarning and keeps running
The rejection is swallowed silently because nobody awaited it
The error is passed to the nearest try/catch in the caller
questions.why: Since Node 15 the default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` mode turns an unhandled rejection into an uncaught exception, which ends the process. The warn-and-continue behaviour is what Node 14 and earlier did. Browsers fire an `unhandledrejection` event and log it; either way it is a bug.
questions.asked: Especially in Node: 'why does our service exit with a stack trace nobody can place?'

questions.q: Why does this not catch the error?
choices: An async callback cannot throw, so each rejection is converted to undefined
forEach catches exceptions from its callback internally and discards them
forEach ignores the returned promises, so the try exits before any save settles
The try needs `await items.forEach(...)` so forEach waits for each save
questions.why: Every `save` is called synchronously inside the try, but forEach discards the promises, so the try exits before they settle and the rejections go unhandled. `await items.forEach(...)` awaits `undefined` and changes nothing. Use `for...of` with await for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))`.
questions.asked: One of the top five real-world async bugs, and it looks fine in review.

questions.q: What order do these log?
questions.why: An async function runs synchronously up to its first `await`, so 1 logs immediately rather than after 3. `await null` still yields to the microtask queue, so the rest of the function is queued and 3 logs before 2.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know that `await` always defers, even on a non-promise.

questions.q: How do you cancel an in-flight `fetch`?
choices: Call `.cancel()` on the promise that `fetch` returned to you
Throw inside the `.then()` handler so the request is torn down
You cannot; once sent, you can only ignore the result when it arrives
Pass `controller.signal` to fetch, then call `controller.abort()`
questions.why: Create an `AbortController`, pass `{ signal: controller.signal }` to fetch, and `abort()` rejects the promise with an `AbortError` and tears down the request. Promises have no `.cancel()`, and throwing in `.then` only runs after the response has already arrived.
questions.asked: The practical follow-up to 'how would you stop stale results overwriting fresh ones?'

questions.q: What is wrong with retrying a failed request on every error?
choices: A retried promise re-uses its first rejection, so a retry can never actually succeed
Retries bypass the HTTP cache, so every attempt downloads the full body again
Non-idempotent requests may be applied twice, and 4xx errors fail again identically
Retries run alongside the original request, doubling load while it is in flight
questions.why: Retry only transient failures (network errors, 429, 502/503/504) with backoff; a 400 or 404 fails the same way every time, and retrying a POST can create two orders. A retry makes a new request, so it can succeed; what you cannot do is re-run an already-settled promise.
questions.asked: A very common backend question. The strong answer mentions idempotency keys.

questions.q: What does 'exponential backoff with jitter' mean?
choices: Each retry waits the same fixed delay, plus a random offset to spread load
Each retry waits about twice as long as the last, plus a random offset
Each round doubles the number of retries while keeping the delay fixed
The client waits for the server's Retry-After header, then adds a second
questions.why: Doubling the delay stops you hammering a struggling service. The random jitter stops every client retrying in lockstep and re-creating the spike, the thundering herd. A fixed delay with jitter spreads clients out but keeps hitting a service that needs longer to recover.
questions.asked: The jitter half is the part that distinguishes a considered answer.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: undefined undefined
1 undefined
1 Promise { 1 }
questions.why: Each `.then` returns a new promise resolved with that handler's return value. The first handler has a block body with no `return`, so the second receives `undefined`, not the original 1. Forgetting to return inside a `.then` is a classic chain bug.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand that .then transforms rather than observes.

questions.q: The network request fails. What happens next?
questions.code:
fetch('/api')
  .then((r) => r.json())
  .catch((e) => console.log('caught', e))
  .then(() => console.log('after'));
choices: `catch` logs it, and the final `.then` is skipped because the chain rejected
The error skips `catch`, because it was raised by `fetch` and not by `r.json()`
`catch` logs it and rethrows, so the promise from the final `.then` rejects too
`catch` logs it, and 'after' still runs because catch returned normally
questions.why: A catch handler that returns normally puts the chain back into the fulfilled state, so the next `.then` runs. That is how you recover with a fallback value. A rejection from any earlier step, fetch included, travels down to the first catch; it only rethrows if you `throw` inside it.
questions.asked: It shows whether you can reason about where a chain is fulfilled or rejected, which is what debugging a fallback needs.

questions.q: Does `fetch` reject when the server answers 404?
choices: Yes: any status outside 200 to 299 rejects with an HTTP error
Only in Node; browsers resolve and set `response.ok` to false
No: it resolves with `ok` set to false; only network failures reject
No for 4xx, but a 5xx rejects because the server itself failed
questions.why: fetch resolves whenever it gets a response, and a 404 or 500 is a completed HTTP exchange. Check `response.ok` or `response.status` yourself. Browsers and Node behave the same; the rejecting behaviour people remember comes from axios.
questions.asked: Extremely common, because it produces errors that show up as 'undefined is not a function' deep in render code.

questions.q: What is bounded concurrency and why would you want it?
choices: Running each operation strictly after the previous one so the server sees one at a time
Keeping at most N operations in flight so a service or socket pool is not overwhelmed
Moving each operation onto a Worker thread so that N of them run truly in parallel
Giving each operation a deadline of N ms, after which its promise rejects
questions.why: `Promise.all` over 10,000 items starts 10,000 requests at once and gets you rate-limited or out of sockets. A pool keeps N in flight and starts the next as each finishes. Strictly one at a time is the N = 1 case, safe but slow.
questions.asked: Comes up whenever you say 'I process a batch of records'.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: A C B
A B C
C A B
C B A
questions.why: The promise executor runs synchronously the moment you construct the promise, so A logs first rather than after C. Calling `resolve()` does not run `.then` callbacks immediately; they are microtasks that wait for the current script to finish, so C comes before B.
questions.asked: People assume the executor is deferred. It is not.

questions.q: How do you put a time limit on a promise from an API with no timeout option?
choices: Wrap the call in `setTimeout` so it is abandoned after N ms
`Promise.any` it against a promise that rejects after N ms
Chain `.finally()` with a timer that rejects it after N ms
`Promise.race` it against a promise that rejects after N ms
questions.why: `race` settles on whichever settles first, so the timer's rejection wins if the call is slow. `any` ignores rejections, so the timer could never win. Neither cancels the slow operation; for fetch, pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` so the request itself is torn down.
questions.asked: The good answer adds 'but race doesn't cancel the slow one'.

questions.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism in JavaScript?
choices: JS interleaves waiting work on one thread; parallel CPU work needs Workers or processes
async/await spreads each awaited call across CPU cores, which gives true parallelism
Node runs your callbacks on a thread pool, so CPU-heavy handlers run in parallel
Concurrency is the browser model and parallelism is Node, where each request gets a thread
questions.why: The event loop interleaves waiting operations on a single thread: great for I/O, useless for CPU work. Node's libuv pool runs some I/O and crypto, never your JavaScript callbacks. Move CPU work to a Web Worker, `worker_threads` or another process.
questions.asked: Then: 'what would you do about a slow CPU-bound endpoint?'

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: Error: x
caught
undefined
an unhandled rejection
questions.why: `return await` inside try/catch settles the rejection inside the function, so the catch runs. Plain `return Promise.reject(...)` would hand the rejection to the caller, skip the local catch and leave `f()` rejected, which is where the unhandled-rejection answer comes from.
questions.asked: A genuinely subtle one: 'return await' is not always redundant.

questions.q: What is a race condition in a search-as-you-type data fetch?
choices: Two components fetch the same URL at once, so the server handles the request twice
The response arrives before the component mounts, so the state update is lost
Two users save the same record, and the second write silently replaces the first
An earlier slow response lands after a later fast one and overwrites the fresh results
questions.why: Type 'ab' fast and the request for 'a' can land after the request for 'ab'. Fix it by aborting the previous request or ignoring responses that are not for the current input. Two users overwriting each other is a lost update on the server, a different problem solved with optimistic concurrency.
questions.asked: The React version of this is an entire interview question on its own.

questions.q: What does `queueMicrotask` do that `setTimeout(fn, 0)` does not?
choices: Runs on a background thread, so heavy callbacks do not block the page
Runs once the current task ends, before any pending timer or the next render
Runs synchronously at the call site, like calling the function directly
Runs after pending timers, but skips the 4 ms clamp that nested timers get
questions.why: `queueMicrotask` puts the callback on the microtask queue, which drains before the event loop moves on to timers or rendering. `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is a task, so every microtask beats it, and nested timers are clamped to about 4 ms on top.
questions.asked: It checks that you can apply the task/microtask split to a scheduling choice rather than recite it.

questions.q: Inside a Node callback such as a timer or request handler, when does a `process.nextTick` callback run relative to promise callbacks?
choices: It is an alias for `setImmediate`, run in the check phase
It runs after the promise microtasks, once the phase ends
Its queue is drained before the promise microtask queue
It is scheduled on the libuv thread pool, off the main thread
questions.why: Node keeps a separate nextTick queue and empties it before promise microtasks, so a nextTick scheduled after a `.then` still runs first. `setImmediate` is the one that waits for the check phase. At the top level of an ES module the order looks reversed, because module evaluation itself runs as a microtask. Recursive nextTick calls can starve the event loop.
questions.asked: A Node-specific depth check. Fine to say you avoid nextTick in application code.

questions.q: Inside an async function, what is wrong with this error handling?
choices: Every failure becomes null, so a bug and a missing record look identical
`catch` without a binding is a SyntaxError in ES modules and strict mode
`await` inside `try` stops the catch from seeing rejections from `load()`
The `return` inside `catch` is ignored, so execution falls through below
questions.why: A blanket catch hides programming errors (a typo, a bad query) alongside the expected ones. Catch the failures you can handle, log or rethrow the rest. Optional catch binding has been valid since ES2019, and awaiting inside try is exactly how rejections reach the catch.
questions.asked: Usually phrased as 'what would you change in this code review?'

questions.q: What does an async generator let you do?
choices: Run each `yield` on its own thread, so all the pages are fetched in parallel
Consume values that arrive over time, like API pages, with `for await...of`
Turn any callback-based API into promises without writing a wrapper
Make a synchronous loop non-blocking by yielding to the renderer each step
questions.why: An `async function*` can await between yields, which is the clean way to express pagination: the consumer writes `for await (const user of allUsers())` and never sees the page cursor. It still runs on one thread and fetches one page at a time.
questions.asked: Paginated APIs are everywhere, so hiding the cursor from callers is a practical design skill.

questions.q: Two `await`s in a row, on independent operations. What is the fix?
questions.code:
const user = await getUser(id);
const settings = await getSettings(id);
choices: Drop both `await`s so the two calls run without blocking each other
Wrap each line in its own `try/catch` so neither blocks the other
Nothing: consecutive `await`s already start both requests at once
`const [user, settings] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getSettings(id)])`
questions.why: As written, the second request does not start until the first finishes, doubling latency. `Promise.all` starts both immediately. Dropping the awaits also starts both, but leaves you holding promises instead of data.
questions.asked: A near-guaranteed follow-up to any async question, and easy to spot once you look for it.

questions.q: What are the states of a promise?
choices: pending, then running, then done, and it can be restarted
pending, then fulfilled or rejected, and it can be re-resolved
pending, then fulfilled or rejected, once and permanently
idle until awaited, then running, then fulfilled or rejected
questions.why: A promise settles exactly once and keeps that result forever, so a second `resolve` call does nothing and awaiting the same promise again returns the cached value. It is not lazy either: the work started when the promise was created, not when it was awaited.
questions.asked: It explains why a promise is not a substitute for an observable or an event stream.

questions.q: Why does a clock built by counting `setInterval` ticks drift?
choices: setInterval re-reads the system clock each tick, so clock adjustments shift it
Its callbacks run on a timer thread that is not synchronised with the page
It only drifts in Node, where timers are serviced by the libuv thread pool
A callback can run late while the main thread is busy, so counting ticks accumulates error
questions.why: Timers guarantee a minimum delay, not an exact one: if the main thread is busy the callback runs late, and each late tick adds error. Browsers also throttle timers in background tabs. For a clock or stopwatch, compute elapsed time from a start timestamp instead of counting ticks.
questions.asked: A concrete question with an obviously right fix: never accumulate time by counting intervals.

questions.q: Neither function has a try/catch. What difference does the `await` make?
questions.code:
async function viaAwait(id) { return await fetchUser(id); }
async function direct(id) { return fetchUser(id); }
choices: `viaAwait` resolves to the raw user, so its caller no longer needs to await it
The caller gets the same result; `viaAwait` also shows up in async stack traces
`viaAwait` catches a rejection itself and resolves with undefined instead
`direct` resolves to a promise nested inside a promise, which callers must unwrap
questions.why: Outside try/catch both settle with the same value or rejection, because an async function adopts a returned promise rather than nesting it. The visible difference is debugging: with `return await`, a rejection's stack keeps an `at async viaAwait` frame, which `direct` loses. Inside try/catch the await also changes behaviour.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know why the old 'no-return-await' lint rule was deprecated rather than just repeating it.

questions.q: You need to process 5,000 records against a rate-limited API. What is the right shape?
choices: `Promise.all` over all 5,000 so the batch finishes as fast as possible
A `for...of` loop with `await`, processing one record at a time
A pool of N workers pulling from a queue, backing off on 429 responses
A `setTimeout` per record with a fixed delay so calls are spread out
questions.why: `Promise.all` floods the API and a serial loop is needlessly slow. A bounded pool keeps throughput high while respecting the limit, and honouring 429 and `Retry-After` keeps you from being blocked. Fixed delays ignore how long each call takes and whether the API is pushing back.
questions.asked: A realistic design question; the answer shows whether you have done batch work in production.

questions.q: In an ES module, what order do these log in?
choices: a d c b
a b c d
a c b d
a c d b
questions.why: a is synchronous. Top-level `await null` queues the rest of the module as a microtask, but `queueMicrotask` queued c first, so c runs before d. The timer is a task and comes last. As a CommonJS script this is a SyntaxError, because top-level await needs a module.
questions.asked: It checks that you apply microtask FIFO order to `await` itself, not only to `.then`.

questions.q: Why should a promise-returning function not also accept a callback?
choices: It doubles the error paths, and one failure can surface as both a rejection and a callback
Node deprecated callbacks in v16, so mixing them now logs a runtime warning
A function that returns a promise cannot invoke a callback until it resolves
TypeScript cannot type a function that returns a promise and takes a callback
questions.why: Some older Node libraries did this and produced functions that could both reject and call back with an error, so callers handled failures twice or not at all. Callbacks are not deprecated; pick one contract and use `util.promisify` at the boundary to wrap old code.
questions.asked: It probes API-design judgement: a strong answer talks about one clear contract for callers.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: AbortError
undefined
TimeoutError
AggregateError
questions.why: `AbortSignal.any` aborts as soon as any input aborts and adopts that input's reason. `AbortSignal.timeout` aborts with a `TimeoutError` DOMException, while `controller.abort()` gives `AbortError`, so a fetch with this signal tells a timeout apart from a user cancel. `AggregateError` belongs to `Promise.any`.
questions.asked: It separates people who hand-roll timeout timers from those who compose signals and report timeouts differently from cancels.

questions.q: In Node 24, what happens when this runs?
choices: `done` logs, then the uncaught `boom` error crashes the process
`caught boom` logs, then `done` logs straight after it
`done` logs, then `caught boom` logs when the timer fires
`done` logs, and the error is silently dropped along with the timer
questions.why: The try block only registers the timer and finishes. When the callback throws later it runs on a fresh stack with no try around it, so it is an uncaught exception, which ends a Node process (browsers log it). Put the try/catch inside the callback, or wrap the timer in a promise and await it.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand that try/catch only covers the current call stack, the root of most lost async errors.

questions.q: A bulk import saves 20 rows concurrently and must report which rows failed. Which call fits?
choices: `Promise.allSettled`, then filter the results whose status is `rejected`
`Promise.all` inside try/catch, then read the failed rows from the error
`Promise.any`, then collect the failures from the AggregateError it throws
`Promise.race`, then re-run it on the remaining rows until none are left
questions.why: `allSettled` waits for every row and returns `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }` per input, so you can report each failure and keep the successes. `Promise.all` rejects with only the first error, and `any` throws an AggregateError only if every row fails.
questions.asked: Partial failure in bulk operations is a daily CRUD problem, and the follow-up is how to report it to the user.

questions.q: In Node 24 or a browser, what does this log?
choices: Ada, because the body was already buffered
undefined, because `json()` returns a promise
A TypeError, because `user` is not an object
A SyntaxError, because the body is not yet parsed
questions.why: `res.json()` reads and parses the body asynchronously and returns a promise, and a promise has no `name` property. Write `const user = await res.json();`. The body being in memory does not matter; the method is async regardless.
questions.asked: The most common first bug with fetch: people await the response and forget the body.

questions.q: What is `users` after this line runs?
questions.code: const users = [1, 2].map(async (id) => ({ id }));
choices: An array of two promises, each already fulfilled with an object
An array of two objects, because `map` awaits each async callback
A single promise that resolves to an array of two objects
An array of two promises that stay pending until they are awaited
questions.why: `map` stores whatever the callback returns, and an async callback always returns a promise, so you get an array of promises. Wrap it as `await Promise.all(ids.map(...))` to get the objects. The promises are not lazy: each callback already ran to completion.
questions.asked: Async callbacks in array methods trip up almost every junior, and the fix leads naturally into Promise.all.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: `caught b failed` logs after about 100 ms, once `a` has settled
`caught b failed` logs after about 10 ms, as soon as `b` rejects
Nothing logs: `b`'s rejection is dropped because `a` resolved first
The process exits on an unhandled rejection before `caught` can log
questions.why: `b` rejects at 10 ms while the code is still awaiting `a`, so no handler is attached yet; Node reports an unhandled rejection and exits. The try/catch would only see it at 100 ms. Start both, then `await Promise.all([a, b])`, which attaches handlers to both immediately.
questions.asked: A production crash that passes code review; spotting it shows you know when a rejection counts as handled.

questions.q: The server answers 200 but the response body is not JSON, so `r.json()` rejects. Which log line appears?
choices: network, since the second argument of then catches the json() failure too
user undefined, since the rejection is converted to undefined by then
Neither: the json() rejection skips both handlers and goes unhandled
user, then network, because both then handlers run for a settled promise
questions.why: The rejection handler passed as the second argument of `.then` only covers the promise it was attached to (the fetch), not errors thrown by the fulfilment handler beside it. `r.json()` rejects inside that handler, so the returned promise rejects, the next `.then` has no rejection handler, and the error goes unhandled. A trailing `.catch` covers both.
questions.asked: The `.then(ok, fail)` versus `.then(ok).catch(fail)` difference is a favourite because it looks equivalent and is not.

questions.q: In Node 24 or a browser, what order do these log?
choices: p1 t1 p2 t2
t1 p2 t2 p1
p1 t1 t2 p2
t1 t2 p1 p2
questions.why: The microtask queue drains after every task, not just after the script, so `p2` (queued inside the first timer) runs before the second timer. `p1 t1 t2 p2` was Node's behaviour before version 11, when it ran all expired timers as a batch; modern Node matches browsers.
questions.asked: It checks that you know microtasks drain between every pair of tasks, which is what makes promise code inside timers and event handlers predictable.

questions.q: Two independent promise chains start in the same task. What order do they log?
questions.code:
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('a1')).then(() => console.log('a2'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('b1')).then(() => console.log('b2'));
choices: b1 b2 a1 a2
a1 b1 b2 a2
a1 a2 b1 b2
a1 b1 a2 b2
questions.why: Each `.then` callback is queued only when the promise before it settles. Both first steps are queued up front, so `a1` and `b1` run first; each of those then queues its second step at the back of the queue. A chain does not run to the end in one go, which is what `a1 a2 b1 b2` assumes.
questions.asked: Interleaving is why two async flows that share state can see each other half-finished, even on one thread.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what order do these log?
choices: B A C
A C B
B C A
A B C
questions.why: Returning a promise from an async function makes the engine adopt it through that promise's `then`, which costs two extra microtask hops, so `A` arrives after the two-step chain `C`. `A B C` assumes an async function hands the inner promise straight back; it never does, because an async function always returns a fresh promise.
questions.asked: Nobody should depend on this ordering; a strong answer says so, and explains that returning a promise adopts it rather than passing it through.

questions.q: In a browser tab or Node 24, what happens when this runs?
choices: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, after a few thousand calls
'timer' never logs: the microtask queue never empties, so nothing else runs
'timer' logs once the engine yields to tasks every thousand or so microtasks
'timer' logs almost at once, because a due timer outranks microtasks
questions.why: Each microtask queues another, and the event loop only moves to the next task once the microtask queue is empty, so the timer, rendering and input all starve while the CPU spins. There is no stack overflow, because each call starts on an empty stack, and no engine inserts yield points into the microtask queue.
questions.asked: The same starvation happens with a promise chain that recursively calls itself, and interviewers like candidates who know promises are not automatically "non-blocking".

questions.q: What does `setTimeout(fn, 1000)` actually guarantee?
choices: `fn` runs no sooner than 1000 ms later, once the stack and earlier tasks clear
`fn` runs within 1000 ms, and sooner if the event loop happens to be idle
`fn` runs 1000 ms later on a timer thread, in parallel with the main thread
`fn` runs exactly 1000 ms later, preempting any code that is running then
questions.why: The delay is a minimum: when it expires the callback is queued as a task, and it waits behind the running code and any earlier tasks. JavaScript never preempts running code, and the callback runs on the same main thread, not a timer thread.
questions.asked: It is the root of every "my timeout fired late" bug report, and a good answer mentions background-tab throttling too.

questions.q: In Node 24, what does this log?
choices: true, and then 'loop done'
false, and then 'loop done'
'loop done', and then false
'loop done', and then true
questions.why: The timer expires at 100 ms but cannot run until the synchronous loop, and the rest of the script, finish, so it fires after 'loop done' having waited at least 500 ms. Nothing interrupts running JavaScript, which is why a busy loop delays every timer, promise and request callback in the process.
questions.asked: It is the smallest demonstration of blocking the event loop, the cause of most "the server stopped answering" incidents in Node.

questions.q: In a browser, why does the user never see "Loading…" on the button?
choices: The DOM batches writes to the same node and keeps only the last one per frame
textContent updates are asynchronous, so the first one is still queued at the end
The browser only paints between tasks, and this task holds the thread until Done
The report runs first, because the engine hoists long synchronous calls to the top
questions.why: Rendering is a step of the event loop that only happens when the current task (and its microtasks) finishes; by then the text is already 'Done'. The DOM write itself was immediate. Fixes are to yield before the heavy work (await `scheduler.yield()` or a `setTimeout`) or move the work to a Web Worker.
questions.asked: It connects the event loop to what users see, and the follow-up is how you would keep the page responsive during the work.

questions.q: What does this log?

no
undefined
Promise { <pending> }

questions.asked: It catches the belief that a resolved promise runs its callbacks immediately, which leads to reading state that has not been set yet.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: ok first
ok first, then an unhandled error
err third
err second
questions.why: A promise settles once: the first `resolve` wins, and later `reject` calls, and even a throw inside the executor, are silently ignored. That silence is the danger, since an error thrown after an early `resolve` in your own wrapper simply disappears.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know a promise is settled exactly once, which matters when you wrap callback APIs that can call back twice.

questions.q: What does this log, and when?
choices: undefined, immediately

Promise { <pending> }, immediately

questions.why: Resolving a promise with another promise (or any thenable) makes it follow that promise, so `outer` settles when `inner` does, with its value. Promises never nest: you can't get a promise of a promise, which is also why returning a promise from `.then` flattens.
questions.asked: Knowing that `resolve` adopts thenables explains flattening in `.then`, `await` and async return values in one idea.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?

undefined, because `then` returned nothing
'then called', then 42
the object itself, since it isn't a real Promise

questions.asked: It probes whether you know await works on duck-typed thenables, the reason query builders like Knex can be awaited directly.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.code: Promise.resolve(1).then(2).then((v) => console.log(v));
choices: undefined
TypeError: 2 is not a function
questions.why: `then` ignores any argument that is not a function and passes the value through unchanged, so 1 reaches the last callback. No TypeError is thrown; the realistic version of this bug is `.then(doSomething())`, which calls the function immediately and passes its result in.
questions.asked: The bug it models, `.then(fn())` instead of `.then(fn)`, turns up in real code review.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: 'data'
Promise { 'data' }
'ignored'
undefined
questions.why: `finally` is for cleanup: its callback gets no argument and its return value is ignored, so the original value passes through. Only a throw (or a rejected promise) from inside `finally` changes the outcome, and then the chain rejects with that error.
questions.asked: It checks you would use `finally` for hiding a spinner or releasing a lock without accidentally changing the result.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: fetch failed, then cleanup failed
Nothing: the cleanup error is unhandled
fetch failed
cleanup failed
questions.why: An error thrown inside `finally` replaces whatever the chain was carrying, so the original 'fetch failed' is lost. Cleanup code that can fail should catch its own errors, or you will spend an incident debugging the wrong message.
questions.asked: It is the promise version of a masked exception, and strong candidates mention the same trap in try/finally.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: Promise { <pending> }

questions.why: When a `.then` callback returns a promise, the next step waits for it and receives its value, so the chain logs 2 after 10 ms. This flattening is what makes sequential async steps possible without nesting.
questions.asked: It is the basic contract of a promise chain; weak answers expect a nested promise to be logged.

questions.q: `sendEmail` returns a promise. What is wrong with this chain?
choices: 'all done' never logs, because the braces make the callback return undefined
'all done' can log before the email is sent, and a failed send is unhandled
The chain runs sendEmail twice, once per `.then`, because callbacks are replayed
Nothing: a promise created inside `.then` is awaited automatically by the chain
questions.why: Without `return`, the callback returns undefined, so the next step runs immediately and the email's promise floats free; if it rejects, nothing handles it. Arrow functions with braces need an explicit `return`. The chain does still continue, which is why the bug goes unnoticed.
questions.asked: The missing `return` in a `.then` is one of the most common real promise bugs; the linter rule for it is `promise/always-return` or TypeScript-ESLint `no-floating-promises`.

questions.q: In a browser, a promise rejects and nothing handles it. What happens?
choices: The console logs 'Uncaught (in promise)', window gets `unhandledrejection`, and the page runs on
The rejection is dropped silently, since browsers only report synchronous errors
The browser retries the operation once and then throws inside the next task
The tab reloads, because the browser treats it like an uncaught exception
questions.why: Browsers report it (console plus the `unhandledrejection` event, which is where error trackers such as Sentry hook in) but keep the page alive. Node 24 is the strict one: its default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` crashes the process.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know where unhandled async errors go in production front-ends, and how you would find out about them.

questions.q: What does 'run-to-completion' mean for JavaScript?
choices: The engine finishes every pending promise before it executes new events
A script runs completely before any module it imports is evaluated
Each async function must finish before the next async function can start
Once a function starts, no other JS runs until it returns or hits an await
questions.why: Nothing can interrupt synchronous JavaScript: event handlers, timers and promise callbacks all wait for the current code to reach a stopping point. `await` is such a point, so an async function can pause while others start; the one-at-a-time rule applies to synchronous stretches, not whole async functions.
questions.asked: It underpins why you never need locks for synchronous code in JavaScript, and why you do need care across `await`.

questions.q: `syncInventory()` usually takes 2 s but sometimes 8 s. What goes wrong?
choices: The interval pauses until the promise settles, so it drifts to 13 s between runs
Node throws, because setInterval callbacks are not allowed to return a promise
Slow runs overlap the next one; schedule the next run with setTimeout after the await
setInterval skips a tick whenever the callback is async, so runs are lost silently
questions.why: setInterval ignores the returned promise and fires every 5 s regardless, so an 8 s run overlaps the next, and two syncs race on the same data. A self-rescheduling `setTimeout` (or a loop with `await sleep(5000)`) waits for each run to finish. It never pauses or skips on its own.
questions.asked: Polling jobs that overlap are a classic production bug; the fix shows you think about what happens when work is slower than expected.

questions.q: In Node 24, what happens when this ES module file runs?
choices: It logs 'start', then throws ReferenceError when load() is eventually called
SyntaxError at parse time, so not even the first line runs
It logs 'start', and `data` would be a pending promise if load() were called
It logs 'start'; `load` is made async implicitly because it contains await
questions.why: `await` is only valid inside an async function (or at the top level of a module), so this is a parse error and the whole file is rejected before anything executes. Parse-time errors are why the log line does not appear, unlike a runtime error thrown later.
questions.asked: An easy warm-up that checks you can read the error and know await needs an async context.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: granted
TypeError: condition is a Promise
Nothing until the promise settles
denied
questions.why: Without `await`, the condition is a Promise object, and every object is truthy, so this grants access to everyone. Nothing throws, which is what makes a missing await in a permission check a security bug; TypeScript-ESLint `no-misused-promises` catches it.
questions.asked: It is a short way to test whether you understand what an async function returns, with a real-world consequence.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.code:
const active = [1, 2, 3].filter(async (id) => id !== 2);
console.log(active);
choices: Promise { [ 1, 3 ] }
questions.why: `filter` is synchronous and keeps an element when the callback's return value is truthy; an async callback returns a promise, which is always truthy. Compute the booleans first with `await Promise.all(ids.map(check))`, then filter by index.
questions.asked: It checks that you know array methods do not await, which also breaks `some`, `every`, `find` and `reduce` with async callbacks.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.code:
async function getName() { return 'Ada'; }
console.log(`Hello ${getName()}`);
choices: Hello Ada
Hello undefined
Hello [object Promise]
Hello Promise { Ada }
questions.why: `getName()` returns a Promise, and interpolating an object calls its `toString`, giving '[object Promise]'. You need `await getName()` first; this exact string showing up in a UI or email is a tell-tale missing await.
questions.asked: Recognising "[object Promise]" in output is a practical debugging skill interviewers like to see.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
questions.code: const users = await fetch('https://api.example.com/users').json();
choices: `users` is a pending promise, because `json()` is itself async
TypeError: `.json` is not a function, since it is called on a Promise
SyntaxError, because `await` cannot prefix a method chain
`users` is the parsed JSON, since the await applies to the whole chain
questions.why: Member access binds tighter than `await`, so `.json()` is called on the Promise that `fetch` returned, which has no such method. Write `const res = await fetch(url); const users = await res.json();` or wrap the first await in parentheses.
questions.asked: Operator precedence around await trips up juniors, and the error message is worth recognising on sight.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: 'no throw', then the process exits on an unhandled rejection
'no throw', and the error is dropped silently
'caught', then an unhandled rejection warning
'caught', because JSON.parse throws synchronously
questions.why: Inside an async function every throw, even a synchronous one, becomes a rejection of the returned promise. The un-awaited call returns normally, the try block completes, and the rejection goes unhandled, which crashes Node 24 by default. `await parse(...)` makes the catch work.
questions.asked: It separates people who know try/catch only sees rejections you await from people who think it catches anything inside the block.

questions.q: In Node 24, what happens when this runs?
choices: 'after', then 'handled'
'handled', then 'after'
'after' only; error swallowed
Uncaught TypeError; no logs
questions.why: `loadUser` is not async, so the guard throws synchronously before any promise exists and `.catch` is never reached. A function that returns promises should fail through a rejection: mark it `async`, or wrap the body with `Promise.try` (ES2025, in Node 24).
questions.asked: The 'sometimes throws, sometimes rejects' function is a real API design flaw; a strong answer names the fix and why callers need one failure channel.

questions.q: A `Db` class is only usable after an async `connect()`. How should you construct it?
choices: Await connect inside a normal constructor; `new` pauses until that promise settles
Write `async constructor()`, and `await new Db()` resolves once connect finishes
Use a static async `create()` that builds the instance, awaits connect, returns it
Call connect in the constructor and make every method check a `ready` flag first
questions.why: Constructors cannot be async (`async constructor` is a SyntaxError), and `await` inside a normal constructor is not allowed either. A static factory keeps the invariant 'if you have a Db, it is connected'; a ready flag technically works but pushes the check into every method and races on first use.
questions.asked: It shows whether you can design around a language limit, which comes up with database clients, SDKs and anything that needs async initialisation.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), roughly how long does this take to reach the last line?
choices: About 0 ms
About 100 ms
About 200 ms
About 400 ms
questions.why: Both timers start when `sleep` is called, not when it is awaited, so they run concurrently and `await b` finds b already done: about 200 ms in total. 400 would need `await sleep(200)` twice. The work starts at the call; `await` only waits for the result.
questions.asked: Understanding that promises are eager is the key to writing concurrent code without Promise.all, and to spotting accidental serialisation.

questions.q: In Node 24, what is wrong with this `sleep` helper?
questions.code: const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve(), ms));
choices: It resolves immediately: `resolve()` runs now and its result goes to setTimeout
It never resolves, because setTimeout receives undefined and ignores it silently
Nothing: `resolve()` is evaluated lazily once the timer has elapsed
It rejects with a TypeError that setTimeout throws for a missing callback
questions.why: The parentheses call `resolve` straight away, fulfilling the promise; setTimeout then throws for its undefined callback, but a throw inside the executor after resolve is ignored. So `await sleep(500)` returns at once with no error. Pass the function itself: `setTimeout(resolve, ms)`.
questions.asked: A small bug with a silent failure mode; it tests whether you can read a callback being called versus passed.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: It throws: two writers hit the same variable
questions.why: Both calls read 10 before either writes, then both write 9: a lost update. Single-threaded does not mean race-free, because every `await` lets another flow run between the read and the write. The real-world fix is an atomic update in the database (`SET stock = stock - 1`) or a per-key lock.
questions.asked: It tests the 'JavaScript is single-threaded so there are no races' myth, which fails the moment the read and write are separate awaits.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const r = await Promise.all([1, Promise.resolve(2), 'x']);
console.log(r);
choices: [ 1, Promise { 2 }, 'x' ]
TypeError: 1 is not a promise
questions.why: Every combinator runs each entry through `Promise.resolve`, so plain values count as already-fulfilled promises and nested promises are unwrapped. That is handy when some entries come from a cache and some from the network.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know combinators accept any iterable of values, not only promises.

questions.q: `ids` turned out to be empty. What happens?
choices: 'all []' and 'race undefined', at once
'all []' logs; race stays pending forever
A RangeError from each, for empty input
Neither logs; empty input leaves them pending
questions.why: `Promise.all([])` fulfils immediately with an empty array, because there is nothing to wait for. `Promise.race([])` has no entrant that could ever settle it, so anything awaiting it hangs; guard empty input before racing. `Promise.any([])` rejects with an AggregateError instead.
questions.asked: Edge cases on empty input are where a race-based timeout helper quietly hangs a request forever.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const wait = (v, ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
console.log(await Promise.all([wait('slow', 60), wait('fast', 10)]));
choices: [ 'slow', 'fast' ]
[ 'fast', undefined ]
[ 'slow' ]
[ 'fast', 'slow' ]
questions.why: `Promise.all` puts each result at its input's index, whatever order they finish in, so you can destructure results positionally. `[ 'fast', 'slow' ]` is completion order, which Promise.all deliberately does not use.
questions.asked: Destructuring `const [user, orders] = await Promise.all(...)` depends on this guarantee.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: TypeError 2
Error 2
AggregateError 1
AggregateError 2
questions.why: `Promise.any` only rejects when every input rejects, and it then rejects with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` array holds each reason in input order. Catch code that only reads `e.message` loses the individual causes.
questions.asked: It checks you know how to report failures from a fallback chain, such as trying three mirrors.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const r = await Promise.allSettled([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject(new Error('no'))]);
console.log(r.map((x) => x.status + ':' + (x.value ?? x.reason.message)));
choices: [ 'fulfilled:1', 'rejected:Error: no' ]
[ 'ok:1', 'error:no' ]
[ 'fulfilled:1', 'rejected:no' ]
[ 'resolved:1', 'rejected:no' ]
questions.why: Each settled result is `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`. 'Resolved' is not a status: a promise can be resolved to another promise and still be pending, which is why the spec uses 'fulfilled'.
questions.asked: Knowing the exact shape means you can filter failures without a trip to the docs in a live exercise.

questions.q: You wrap a slow `fetch` in `Promise.race` against a 5-second timeout, and the timeout wins. What happens to the request?
choices: The losing promise is cancelled, so its socket is closed with a reset
It keeps running; the response is just ignored unless you abort it
It is paused, and resumes if you await the same fetch promise again
It rejects with an AbortError the moment the race settles
questions.why: Promises have no cancellation: `race` just stops listening to the loser, so the request still uses a connection and the server still does the work. Pass an `AbortSignal` (for example `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`) to fetch so the timeout actually tears it down.
questions.asked: It separates 'I stopped waiting' from 'I stopped the work', which matters for server load and for non-idempotent requests.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: 'caught a', then 'still alive'
'caught a', then a crash on unhandled 'b'
'caught b', then 'still alive'
'caught a' and 'caught b', then 'still alive'
questions.why: `Promise.all` attaches a handler to every input up front, so the later rejection of 'b' counts as handled even though it is ignored. Contrast awaiting two promises one after another, where the second can reject before anything listens and crash Node.
questions.asked: It tests a precise model of what "handled" means, which explains why Promise.all is safer than sequential awaits on pre-started work.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: An unhandled rejection
'AggregateError'
'mirror B'
'mirror A down'
questions.why: `race` settles with whichever input settles first, and a rejection counts, so the quick failure wins. If you want the first success and to ignore failures, that is `Promise.any`.
questions.asked: Confusing race with any is a common bug in fallback and mirror logic.

questions.q: `const parts = { user: getUser(), orders: getOrders() }` holds two promises. Which awaits both concurrently and keeps the keys?
choices: `await Promise.allSettled(parts)`, which maps each key to its settled result
`await Promise.all(parts)`, since `all` accepts an object and resolves each value
`Object.fromEntries` over `Promise.all` of the entries mapped to `[k, await p]`
`await Promise.all(Object.values(parts))`, which returns an object with the same keys
questions.why: The combinators take iterables and return arrays, so an object is rejected with a TypeError ('object is not iterable'). Mapping entries to `async ([k, p]) => [k, await p]`, awaiting them with `Promise.all`, and rebuilding with `Object.fromEntries` keeps the names; `Object.values` loses them.
questions.asked: It shows you can compose the standard library instead of reaching for a utility package for a five-line need.

questions.q: What does this code do with the list of user ids?
choices: Starts every save at once and waits for all of them, like Promise.all
Runs the saves one after another, stopping at the first rejection
Runs them one after another, skipping failures and carrying on
Only the final save is awaited; the rest run unobserved in the background
questions.why: Each step chains onto the previous promise, so `saveUser(id)` for the next id only starts when the last one has fulfilled, and a rejection skips every later `.then`. It predates async/await; a `for...of` loop with `await` says the same thing more readably.
questions.asked: You will meet this idiom in older codebases, and a strong answer offers the for...of rewrite.

questions.q: Which wraps a Node-style callback API `readConfig(path, (err, data) => ...)` as a promise?
choices: `new Promise((res, rej) => readConfig(p, (err, d) => (err ? rej(err) : res(d))))`
`new Promise((res) => res(readConfig(p, (err, d) => d)))`, resolving on return
`new Promise((res, rej) => readConfig(p).then(res, rej))`, reusing its promise
`Promise.resolve(readConfig(p, (err, d) => (err ? err : d)))`, which waits for it
questions.why: A callback API returns nothing useful, so you must settle the promise from inside the callback, routing `err` to reject. The other versions resolve with the function's synchronous return value (undefined) or assume it already returns a promise. In Node, `util.promisify` does this for you.
questions.asked: Promisifying a callback API is a common live-coding warm-up, and the error branch is what they are watching for.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: 'caught', then an unhandled-rejection warning as well
Nothing logs, and the error is silently discarded
'caught', because any executor error rejects the promise
Nothing logs; p never settles, error unhandled
questions.why: An async executor returns a promise that `new Promise` ignores: the throw rejects that hidden promise instead of `p`, so `p` never settles and the SyntaxError surfaces as an unhandled rejection, crashing Node 24. Never pass an async function to `new Promise`; write an async function instead.
questions.asked: The async-executor anti-pattern is flagged by ESLint `no-async-promise-executor`; interviewers like candidates who can explain why.

questions.q: `hide()` removes the spinner. Which guarantees it runs whether `loadOrders()` succeeds or fails?
choices: `loadOrders().then(() => hide());` with no catch
`try { await loadOrders(); hide(); } catch {}`
`try { await loadOrders(); } finally { hide(); }`
`await loadOrders();` followed by `hide();` on the next line
questions.why: `finally` runs after success and after an awaited rejection, which is exactly the cleanup contract. The other versions skip `hide()` whenever the load fails, leaving a spinner that never stops; the empty catch also hides the error.
questions.asked: Stuck spinners are the most visible async bug in a CRUD UI, and finally is the simplest fix.

questions.q: `fetchUser` rejects. In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: The error is logged, and `user.name` logs 'undefined'
The error is logged, then a TypeError reading `name` of undefined
The rejection propagates to the top level, so `user.name` never runs
The error is logged, and `user` is an empty object with no name
questions.why: `.catch(console.error)` handles the rejection and resolves with console.error's return value, undefined, so the caller carries on with no user and fails later with a less helpful error. Log and rethrow, or return an explicit value the caller must check.
questions.asked: Catch-and-log-and-continue is a common smell; interviewers want to hear 'handle it where you can do something useful'.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: false true
true false
false false
true true
questions.why: An async function always creates and returns a new promise, which follows the returned one; a plain function hands back the same object. It matters when you cache promises for de-duplication, because wrapping the getter in `async` makes every call a new object.
questions.asked: It tests your mental model of what `async` adds to a function, beyond making await legal.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const wait = (v, ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
for await (const v of [wait('a', 50), wait('b', 10)]) console.log(v);
choices: a
TypeError: array is not async iterable
b a
a b
questions.why: `for await` over a plain array awaits each element in index order, so it waits 50 ms for 'a' and then finds 'b' already done. It does not yield in completion order; for that you would race the remaining promises yourself.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know `for await` works on sync iterables of promises and what order it gives you.

questions.q: Ten components call `getConfig()` at once during start-up. Which design makes one request and still lets a failed load be retried later?
choices: Debounce `getConfig` so only the last call within 100 ms actually runs a request
Cache the resolved value after the first await and return it to later callers
Cache the promise, and drop it on rejection so a later call retries
Cache the promise forever, so every caller shares one pending or settled request
questions.why: All ten calls arrive before the first response, so caching the value still fires ten requests; caching the in-flight promise shares one. Caching it forever also caches a failure, so drop it on rejection. A debounce would leave nine callers with nothing.
questions.asked: Request de-duplication is how token refresh and config loading avoid stampedes, and it is what React Query does internally.

questions.q: In this concurrency limiter, why can the workers share `next` without a lock?
choices: Each worker closes over its own copy of `next`, so nothing is shared
No await sits between the check and `next++`, so nothing interleaves
`++` on a `let` is atomic in V8, as it would be with an Atomics call
Promise.all runs the workers one at a time, so they never overlap
questions.why: Only one piece of JavaScript runs at a time and it can only be interrupted at an `await`. The comparison and the increment happen in one synchronous stretch, so two workers can never take the same index. Put an await between them and you would get duplicates.
questions.asked: Writing a promise pool is a common take-home; explaining why the shared counter is safe shows real event-loop understanding.

questions.q: Using the same `pool(items, 3, fn)`, `fn` rejects for item 5 of 100. What happens?
choices: The pool promise rejects at once, but the other two workers keep processing items
The failing worker retries item 5 until it succeeds, then continues
The pool promise resolves once all 100 items have been attempted, ignoring the error
The pool stops all workers immediately and no more items are processed
questions.why: The failed worker exits its loop, so `Promise.all` rejects immediately, but nothing stops the other workers, which carry on through the list with nobody awaiting them. Decide the policy explicitly: catch per item and collect failures, or share an AbortSignal so workers stop.
questions.asked: Error semantics are what separate a toy pool from one you would trust in a batch job.

questions.q: You upload 1,000 files in chunks of 10 with `await Promise.all(chunk.map(upload))` per chunk. Why is a pool of 10 usually faster?
choices: Promise.all runs a chunk sequentially, while a pool runs its slots in parallel
A pool compresses uploads in the background while earlier ones are in flight
A pool reuses one TCP connection, while each chunk opens ten new ones
Each chunk waits on its slowest file; a pool refills a slot at once
questions.why: With chunking, one slow file holds nine idle slots until it finishes, so total time is the sum of each chunk's slowest item. A pool keeps all ten slots busy continuously. Connection reuse is the same either way, and Promise.all does start everything concurrently.
questions.asked: It checks that you can reason about utilisation, not just "limit to N".

questions.q: A Node 24 script runs `await Promise.all(urls.map((u) => fetch(u)))` over 20,000 URLs. What typically goes wrong?
choices: Promise.all rejects arrays over 10,000 entries with a RangeError
They run one at a time, because fetch shares a single socket
All start at once: sockets, memory and rate limits all suffer
fetch queues them internally at six per host, so it is slow but safe
questions.why: Every request starts immediately, so you hold 20,000 pending responses, exhaust sockets or file descriptors, and trip the remote's rate limits; one failure then rejects the whole batch while the rest keep running. The six-per-host limit is a browser HTTP/1.1 rule, not something Node's fetch applies for you.
questions.asked: It is the classic 'works on 10 items, falls over on 20,000' bug, and the answer should mention a concurrency limit and per-item error handling.

questions.q: Saves for the same document must never overlap, but different documents may save at the same time. Which structure fits?
choices: One global mutex around every save, released when the save settles
A Map from document id to the promise of its latest queued save
A debounce per document, so only the latest save within a window runs
Promise.all over each document's pending saves, started together
questions.why: Chaining each new save onto that document's last promise (`tail = tail.then(save, save)`) serialises per key while other keys proceed. A global mutex serialises everything; a debounce drops intermediate saves, which is fine for autosave drafts but not for an ordered log of changes.
questions.asked: Per-key queues are how you prevent out-of-order writes without killing throughput, and the idea transfers to job queues.

questions.q: `fn` always rejects. How many times is it called?
choices: Forever, since the loop has no exit
questions.why: With `<=`, attempts 0 to 3 run: one initial call plus three retries, and the last failure is rethrown. Be explicit in naming (`maxAttempts` versus `retries`); off-by-one here means one extra call to a service that is already struggling.
questions.asked: A small reading exercise that shows care with loop bounds in code that talks to other systems.

questions.q: `fn` returns a promise that rejects. How many times does `withRetry` call it?
questions.why: `return fn()` returns the promise without awaiting it, so the try block is left before the rejection happens and the catch never sees it: one call, and the caller gets the rejection. `return await fn()` keeps the rejection inside the try, which is the one place `return await` changes behaviour.
questions.asked: Retry helpers that never retry pass unit tests with synchronous fakes; spotting this shows you understand where rejections surface.

questions.q: Which failures should an HTTP client retry automatically?
choices: Any 4xx or 5xx response, since the server may have recovered by then
Only 500, because 502, 503 and 504 mean the server is permanently down
Network errors, 408, 429, 502, 503 and 504, honouring any Retry-After
400 and 422 as well, since validation might pass on a second attempt
questions.why: Retry what is transient: dropped connections, timeouts, rate limits and gateway or overload errors. A 400, 401, 404 or 422 fails identically every time. Even on retryable codes, only retry non-idempotent requests like POST when they carry an idempotency key.
questions.asked: It shows you know retries can make an outage worse, and which status codes actually signal "try again".

questions.q: A request returns 429 with `Retry-After: 30`. What should your client do?
choices: Retry at once with backoff starting at 100 ms, since 429 is always brief
Wait at least 30 s; the header can also be an HTTP date instead
Treat it as permanent and surface a failure, since the client was rejected
Wait 30 milliseconds, because Retry-After is given in milliseconds
questions.why: RFC 9110 defines Retry-After as either delay-seconds or an HTTP date; the server is telling you exactly when it will accept you again. Retrying sooner just earns more 429s and may extend a ban. Use your own backoff only when the header is absent.
questions.asked: Integrations with Stripe, GitHub and most SaaS APIs depend on respecting rate-limit headers.

questions.q: What delay does this backoff give on attempt 3?
questions.code: const delay = (attempt) => Math.random() * Math.min(30_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
choices: Between 0 and 4,000 ms
Between 4,000 and 30,000 ms
Between 0 and 1,500 ms
Exactly 4,000 ms
questions.why: 500 × 2³ is 4,000, which is under the 30 s cap, and `Math.random()` scales it to a random point from 0 to 4,000 ms: 'full jitter'. The randomness spreads out clients that all failed at the same moment, so they don't retry in lockstep.
questions.asked: Reading a backoff formula and naming the cap shows you could implement one yourself.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens after "done" is logged?
choices: The process crashes 5 s later with an unhandled "timeout" rejection
The process stays alive forever, because the timeout promise never settles
The process exits at once, since nothing awaits the timeout promise any more
The process stays alive about 5 s until the timer fires, then exits normally
questions.why: The pending timer keeps Node's event loop alive, and when it fires the rejection is already handled by `race`, so the process exits cleanly but 5 s late. In a server the same leak piles up one live timer per request. Clear the timer in a `finally`, or use `AbortSignal.timeout`.
questions.asked: Timeout helpers that leak timers are a real cause of slow test runs and 'Jest did not exit' warnings.

questions.q: In a retry loop, what is the difference between a per-attempt timeout and an overall deadline?
choices: The deadline is enforced by the server, the per-attempt timeout by the client
They are the same thing; one is the other multiplied by the attempt count
Per-attempt caps one call; the deadline caps the total, backoff included
Per-attempt covers backoff waits; the deadline covers only time on the network
questions.why: Without a deadline, three 10 s attempts plus backoff can keep a user waiting 40 s; without a per-attempt timeout, one hung call eats the whole budget. Combine them: a fresh `AbortSignal.timeout` per attempt, merged with the deadline signal via `AbortSignal.any`.
questions.asked: It shows you think about latency from the caller's point of view, not just about making the call eventually succeed.

questions.q: The user navigates away and `signal` aborts mid-request. What is wrong with this retry loop?
choices: Nothing: an aborted fetch resolves with an empty response, which ends the loop
It retries a deliberate cancellation; rethrow at once when `e.name` is AbortError
It loops forever, because an aborted signal makes fetch hang instead of rejecting
It retries correctly, since each attempt creates a fresh signal automatically
questions.why: An abort is the caller saying 'stop', not a transient failure: this loop sleeps through backoff and reports a failure instead of a cancellation. With the same aborted signal, every retry also rejects instantly. Check for AbortError (and the signal's reason) and rethrow immediately.
questions.asked: Cancellation-aware retries are the difference between a retry helper and a production-ready one.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: AbortError
TimeoutError
TypeError
CancelError
questions.why: Aborting with no reason rejects the fetch with a DOMException named 'AbortError'; `AbortSignal.timeout` produces 'TimeoutError' instead, and a network failure is a TypeError. Checking `e.name` is how you tell a deliberate cancel apart from a real failure.
questions.asked: Error handling code that shows a red "request failed" banner for a cancelled request is a common UX bug.

questions.q: How do you give a single `fetch` a 5-second timeout in current browsers and Node 24?
choices: `setTimeout(() => fetch.cancel(url), 5000)` alongside it
`Promise.race` with a 5 s timer, which aborts the loser
`fetch(url, { timeout: 5000 })`, the built-in option
`fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })`
questions.why: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` returns a signal that aborts itself with a TimeoutError, and fetch tears the request down when it fires. fetch has no `timeout` option (it is silently ignored), there is no `fetch.cancel`, and a race only stops you waiting.
questions.asked: Every service call needs a timeout; knowing the one-line modern version is expected.

questions.q: A search box reuses one controller. What happens to the second request?
choices: It runs, but aborts itself automatically after the first response arrives
It runs normally, because `abort()` only affects requests already in flight
It rejects at once with AbortError, because the signal is permanently aborted
It waits until the controller is reset, then runs with the same signal
questions.why: An AbortSignal only goes one way: once aborted it stays aborted, and anything given it later rejects straight away. Create a new AbortController per request (and abort the previous one), which is what a React effect cleanup or a search handler should do.
questions.asked: A 'search stopped working after the first keystroke' bug is usually this.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: TypeError: abort() takes no argument
true 'user left page'
true undefined
false 'user left page'
questions.why: `abort(reason)` stores the reason on `signal.reason`, and APIs such as fetch reject with that reason, so you can tell 'user left page' from a timeout. With no argument the reason is a DOMException named AbortError.
questions.asked: Passing a reason makes cancellations debuggable in logs, and many developers do not know the parameter exists.

questions.q: `importRows(rows, signal)` awaits a database write per row across 50,000 rows. How do you make it stop promptly when the signal aborts?
choices: Call `signal.throwIfAborted()` at the top of each iteration of the loop
Wrap the whole loop in `Promise.race` with a promise that listens for abort
Check `signal.reason` once the loop finishes and roll back if it is set
Nothing extra: a signal passed as a parameter stops the async function by itself
questions.why: A signal is just an object with a flag and an event; your own code must check it. `throwIfAborted()` throws the signal's reason, so the loop exits with the same error fetch would give. A race would stop you awaiting while the writes carry on.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can make your own long-running functions cancellable, not just call fetch with a signal.

questions.q: This cancellable `sleep` is called in a loop with one long-lived signal. What two problems does it have?
choices: It resolves twice on abort and leaks the timer when it completes
Nothing: abort listeners are removed automatically once the promise settles
It rejects with the wrong error and clears the timer too early
It ignores an already-aborted signal and never removes its listener
questions.why: The 'abort' event fires once, so if the signal is already aborted the sleep just waits the full time; check `signal.aborted` first. And each call adds a listener that is never removed, so thousands pile up on the same signal. Use `{ once: true }` and remove it when the timer wins.
questions.asked: Writing an abortable helper correctly is a good senior-leaning exercise; these two bugs are what reviewers look for.

questions.q: The user clicks Cancel while `POST /orders` is in flight, and you abort the fetch. Was the order created?
choices: Yes, always: once fetch has been called the server is certain to finish it
No: aborting the fetch sends the server a cancel that rolls the request back
Maybe: the server may have processed it already, so reconcile with a status check
No: the request body is only sent once the response headers have arrived
questions.why: Aborting only stops the client listening and closes the connection; the server may have committed the order before noticing, or never noticed at all. That is why checkout uses idempotency keys and why the UI should re-check the order's state rather than assume.
questions.asked: It checks you understand cancellation is client-side, which matters for payments and anything non-idempotent.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), `res` arrived, and the body is still streaming. What happens?
choices: `data` is the full JSON, since the abort came after the response
`res.json()` rejects with AbortError: the signal also covers the body
`data` is whatever part of the body had arrived, parsed as far as it goes
`res.json()` hangs forever, waiting for a body that was cut off
questions.why: The signal governs the whole exchange, including reading the body, so aborting after the headers errors the stream and `json()` rejects with the abort reason. That is how you cancel a large download half-way. Once the body has been fully consumed, aborting has no effect.
questions.asked: It shows you know where fetch actually waits: once for headers, again for the body.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: TypeError: body already read
Logs the text, then {}
Logs the text, then undefined
Logs the text, then { a: 1 }
questions.why: A body is a stream that can be consumed once; the second read throws 'Body is unusable'. Parse the text yourself with `JSON.parse(text)`, or call `res.clone()` before the first read when two consumers really need it.
questions.asked: Logging a response body and then parsing it is where people hit this, usually while debugging something else.

questions.q: A DELETE returns `204 No Content`. In Node 24 (ES module), what does this do?
choices: It logs null
It logs an empty object {}
It logs undefined
It throws a SyntaxError
questions.why: `json()` parses the body as JSON, and an empty body is not valid JSON ('Unexpected end of JSON input'). A shared API helper should check for 204 (or an empty body) before calling `json()`, rather than every delete showing an error toast.
questions.asked: Generic fetch wrappers break on 204 all the time; the fix shows you have built one for real.

questions.q: What does the server receive as the body?
choices: Nothing: fetch rejects with a TypeError for a plain-object body
The JSON `{"name":"Ada"}`, with Content-Type application/json
The string `[object Object]`, with Content-Type text/plain
Form fields `name=Ada`, with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded
questions.why: fetch does not serialise objects: a plain object is converted to a string, giving '[object Object]' as text/plain. Send `JSON.stringify(data)` with a `Content-Type: application/json` header; `URLSearchParams` or `FormData` bodies are the ones that get their content type set automatically.
questions.asked: A 400 from your own API with "[object Object]" in the logs is a rite of passage; it tests that you know fetch is low-level.

questions.q: What happens when you call an async generator function like `pages()`?
choices: It returns a promise of an array of every value the body yields
It returns an async generator object; the body waits for the first `next()`
It runs the body up to the first `yield` and returns that value
It runs the body to the end and returns an array of promises
questions.why: Calling any generator only creates the iterator object; nothing in the body runs until something calls `next()`, usually a `for await` loop. That laziness is the point: a paginated fetcher makes no request until someone consumes it.
questions.asked: Laziness is the property that makes async generators good for pagination and streams.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: 1 2 cleanup end
1 2 end cleanup
1 2 3 cleanup end
1 2 end
questions.why: Leaving a `for await` early (break, return or throw) calls the iterator's `return()`, which resumes the generator at its paused `yield` as if it returned, so `finally` runs before the loop statement finishes. That is where you close a cursor or release a stream reader.
questions.asked: It shows whether you trust generators to clean up resources, which matters when they wrap database cursors or connections.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: b b
a undefined
a a
a b
questions.why: An async generator queues `next()` calls and serves them in order, one resumption at a time, so concurrent callers each get the next value. Two callers never see the same item, which makes a shared generator a simple work queue.
questions.asked: It probes whether you know async generators are safe to pull from concurrently, the basis of some worker-pool designs.

questions.q: The first match is on page 2 of 50. How many `api.list` calls does this make?
questions.why: The generator is pulled one page at a time and pauses at `yield`; when the loop breaks after page 2, the generator is closed and never asks for page 3. An eager helper that collected all pages into an array first would make 50 calls.
questions.asked: Lazy pagination saves real API quota, and interviewers like candidates who can say exactly how many calls are made.

questions.q: What does an object need for `for await...of` to consume it?
choices: A `then` method, so the loop can await the object as a whole
A `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` method returning an object whose `next()` returns promises
An `async next()` method directly on the object, with no symbol required
A `length` property and numeric keys whose values are promises
questions.why: `for await` looks up `Symbol.asyncIterator` and falls back to `Symbol.iterator`, awaiting each value. A bare `next` method is not enough, and a thenable is awaited once, not iterated. Streams, Node readables and async generators all implement the async iterator protocol.
questions.asked: Knowing the protocol lets you wrap an event source or SDK cursor so it works with `for await`.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
async function* g() { yield Promise.resolve(42); }
for await (const v of g()) console.log(v);
choices: undefined
Promise { <pending> }
Promise { 42 }
questions.why: `yield` inside an async generator awaits its operand, so consumers receive 42, never a promise. With a sync generator and a plain `for...of`, you would get the promise object itself.
questions.asked: It checks your model of where awaiting happens in async iteration.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: use 1, make 1, use 2, make 2, use 3, make 3
make 1, make 2, use 1, make 3, use 2, use 3
make 1, make 2, make 3, then use 1, use 2, use 3
make 1, use 1, make 2, use 2, make 3, use 3
