questions.why: Async generators are pull-based: the producer pauses at each `yield` until the consumer asks for the next value, so it never runs ahead. That is backpressure for free, the reason a generator over a paginated API or a file does not load everything into memory.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "what if the producer is faster than the consumer?", and the answer is that it simply waits.

questions.q: In Node 24 or a browser, what is `res.body` on a fetch `Response`?
choices: A promise that resolves with the parsed body, like `res.json()` does
A string holding the body, filled in once the download completes
A ReadableStream of Uint8Array chunks, or null when there is no body
A Node Buffer in Node and a Blob in the browser, matching the platform
questions.why: `res.body` is a web ReadableStream of bytes, which is what `text()`, `json()` and `blob()` consume for you. Reading it directly lets you show download progress or process data as it arrives. It is null for bodiless responses such as 204.
questions.asked: It opens the streaming conversation: progress bars, NDJSON, and AI-style token streaming all start from `res.body`.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: { value: 'a', done: false } { value: null, done: true }
{ value: 'a', done: false } { value: undefined, done: true }
{ value: 'a', done: true } { value: undefined, done: true }
{ value: 'a', done: false } { done: true }
questions.why: `read()` resolves with iterator-style results: `done: false` with a value while data remains, then `done: true` once the stream is closed. The chunk that carries data is never marked done, which is why reader loops check `done` before using `value`.
questions.asked: The manual reader loop is still what you write in older browsers or when you need fine control.

questions.q: You need to write an upload stream to storage and hash it at the same time. What does `stream.tee()` give you?
choices: Two branches, each getting every chunk; a slow branch makes the stream buffer for it
Two branches that split the chunks between them, alternating one chunk each
A copy of the whole stream buffered in memory first, then replayed to each reader
A single stream that can now be locked by two readers at the same time
questions.why: `tee()` locks the original and returns two ReadableStreams that both see every chunk. The source is read at the pace of the faster branch, so chunks queue up in memory for the slower one; a hashing branch that stalls can therefore grow memory without bound.
questions.asked: It tests understanding of streams as single-consumer by default, and the memory cost of splitting one.

questions.q: A 2-byte UTF-8 character arrives split across two chunks. What does this log?
choices: A TypeError on the first chunk
'é', decoded correctly
'e', with the accent lost
'��', two replacement characters
questions.why: Each `decode` call without `{ stream: true }` treats its bytes as complete, so half a character becomes U+FFFD twice. `decode(chunk, { stream: true })`, or `TextDecoderStream`, keeps the partial bytes for the next chunk. It only shows up with non-ASCII text, which is why it slips through testing.
questions.asked: Garbled accents in streamed output are a real bug in chat and log viewers; it tests byte versus character thinking.

questions.q: In Node 24, which reads a streamed text response chunk by chunk as strings?
choices: `const r = res.body.getReader('text')`, then `r.read()` in a loop
`for await (const s of res.body)`, since fetch bodies yield strings
`for await (const s of res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()))`
`while (!done) { s = await res.text(); }`, reading one chunk per call
questions.why: `res.body` yields Uint8Array chunks; piping through `TextDecoderStream` decodes them, handling characters split across chunks. `res.text()` reads the whole body once, and `getReader` has no text mode.
questions.asked: Streaming responses from an AI API or a log tail are the everyday use; it tests you can wire up the pieces.

questions.q: This NDJSON reader works in development but fails intermittently in production. Why?
choices: TextDecoderStream sometimes drops the newline characters between records
Chunk boundaries fall mid-line, so JSON.parse gets half a record
JSON.parse cannot run inside a `for await` loop body on large inputs
The server must send each record as its own chunk, or NDJSON is invalid
questions.why: Chunks are sized by the network, not by your records, so a line can be split across two chunks. Keep the text after the last newline in a buffer and prepend it to the next chunk, and flush it at the end. Locally, small fast responses tend to arrive in one chunk, hiding the bug.
questions.asked: 'Works locally, fails over a real network' is a strong hint about chunk boundaries, and interviewers want you to reach for it.

questions.q: What does a ReadableStream's `pull()` callback give you that enqueueing everything in `start()` does not?
choices: The stream calls pull only when its queue is below the high-water mark
pull lets the consumer request a chunk by index rather than in order
pull caches every chunk, so the stream can be read twice by two readers
pull runs on a worker thread, so producing chunks never blocks the page
questions.why: With `pull`, the stream asks for data only when there is room in its internal queue (`desiredSize > 0`), so a slow consumer slows the producer: backpressure. Enqueueing everything in `start` fills memory regardless of whether anyone is reading.
questions.asked: Backpressure is the concept behind every streaming interview question, in browsers and in Node alike.

questions.q: What is the difference between `readable.pipeThrough(t)` and `readable.pipeTo(w)`?
choices: pipeThrough works in browsers only; pipeTo is the Node-only equivalent
pipeThrough buffers the whole stream first; pipeTo streams chunk by chunk
pipeThrough copies chunks; pipeTo moves them and empties the source
pipeThrough returns the transform's readable side; pipeTo returns a promise
questions.why: pipeThrough takes a `{ writable, readable }` pair such as a TransformStream and returns its readable end, so calls chain. pipeTo sends to a WritableStream and returns a promise that settles when the pipe finishes or fails, which is where you catch errors. Both stream with backpressure in both environments.
questions.asked: Composing decode, parse and write steps is how streaming pipelines are built; it shows you can read one.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: ReadableStream { locked: true }
questions.why: Each chunk passes through `transform`, which enqueues the uppercased version on the readable side, and `Array.fromAsync` consumes the stream as an async iterable. Chunks stay separate; nothing concatenates them unless your transform does.
questions.asked: Writing a small TransformStream is the natural next step after reading one, and a quick live exercise.

questions.q: In Node 24, you `for await` over a fetch response's `res.body` and `break` after the first chunk. What happens to the stream?
choices: It stays locked and open until the response object is garbage-collected
The stream is cancelled, so the underlying connection is released
It keeps downloading into memory so a later loop can resume it
It throws a TypeError, since a locked stream cannot be abandoned
questions.why: Breaking out of async iteration calls the iterator's `return()`, which cancels the stream by default and releases the connection; pass `stream.values({ preventCancel: true })` if you only want to release the lock. It is the stream version of a generator's `finally`.
questions.asked: Resource cleanup on early exit is what makes async iteration safer than hand-written reader loops.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: DataCloneError
SyntaxError
Nothing: the method is dropped silently
TypeError
questions.why: The structured clone algorithm copies data, not behaviour, and throws a DOMException named DataCloneError on functions (and DOM nodes). JSON.stringify would silently drop the method instead. The same rule applies to anything you `postMessage` to a worker.
questions.asked: It checks you know what can cross a worker boundary before you design a message format.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: object true | true 1 true
string false | false 0 false
string true | true 1 false
string false | true 1 true
questions.why: The JSON round trip turns the Date into a string, the Set into `{}`, and drops the undefined property. `structuredClone` keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays, undefined values and even cycles. It is the right deep-copy tool for plain data.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "and what can structuredClone not copy?": functions, DOM nodes and class prototypes.

questions.q: You `postMessage` a class instance to a worker. What does this model show arrives?
choices: 250 function false
250 function true
250 undefined false
undefined undefined false
questions.why: Structured clone copies own data properties into a plain object; the prototype chain, and so every method, is lost. Workers should exchange plain data and rebuild rich objects on the other side (for example `Money.fromJSON(msg)`).
questions.asked: It shows you have actually passed data to a worker and hit the missing-method surprise.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: Transferring moves ownership of the memory instead of copying it, so the original buffer is detached (length 0). `worker.postMessage(buf, [buf])` works the same way, which is how you hand a large image or file to a worker in constant time.
questions.asked: Transferables are the key performance idea in worker messaging; strong candidates mention that the sender can no longer use the buffer.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: DataCloneError
TypeError
SyntaxError
Nothing: the method is dropped
questions.why: Structured clone (used by `postMessage`, `structuredClone` and IndexedDB) cannot copy functions, so it throws a DOMException named DataCloneError. It does not silently drop the method the way `JSON.stringify` would, which is why posting a class instance with methods to a worker fails loudly.
questions.asked: The first worker bug most people hit; a good answer says to send plain data and keep the behaviour on each side.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const copy = structuredClone(new Map([['k', { at: new Date(0) }]]));
console.log(copy instanceof Map, copy.get('k').at instanceof Date);
choices: false false
true false
false true
true true
questions.why: Unlike a JSON round trip, structured clone understands built-in types: Map, Set, Date, RegExp, ArrayBuffer, typed arrays and Error all come back as the same kind of object. JSON would turn the Map into `{}` and the Date into a string.
questions.asked: Checks you know why `structuredClone` replaced the `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` deep-copy trick.

questions.q: A worker throws an exception that nothing inside it catches. What does the page see?
choices: A rejected promise from the last `postMessage` call the page made
The page script crashes with the same error at the `new Worker` line
An `error` event on the Worker object; the page itself keeps running
Nothing at all, because worker errors are only visible in its own console
questions.why: Uncaught errors in a dedicated worker are reported to the page as an `error` event on the Worker object (with message, filename and line). `postMessage` returns nothing, so there is no promise to reject; a request/response wrapper must listen for `error` and fail its pending requests itself.
questions.asked: Shows whether you have built error handling around worker messaging rather than just the happy path.

questions.q: Which job belongs in a Web Worker?
choices: Waiting on three slow `fetch` calls so they do not block the page
Parsing and aggregating a 40 MB CSV file the user just dropped in
Updating the DOM table with the rows returned by the API
Debouncing keystrokes in a search box before calling the server
questions.why: Workers help with CPU-bound work that would block the main thread for hundreds of milliseconds, such as parsing a large file. Waiting on the network already doesn't block anything, workers cannot touch the DOM, and debouncing is cheap timer logic.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that async I/O and CPU-heavy work are different problems with different fixes.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what order do these log in?
choices: after call, done, timer
after call, timer, then done later
after call, timer, done
timer, after call, done
questions.why: `async` does not move work off the thread: the loop runs synchronously inside `report()` before 'after call' prints, and the await resumes in a microtask ahead of the timer. Heavy computation needs a worker or chunking, not the `async` keyword.
questions.asked: Catches the belief that marking a function `async` makes it 'run in the background'.

questions.q: You wrap a worker in `call(type, payload)` that returns a promise. Replies can come back in any order. How do you match each reply to its caller?
choices: Create a new Worker per call so each one only ever has one reply
Use `await worker.postMessage(...)`, which resolves with the reply
Resolve the oldest pending promise, since replies arrive in order
Send an id with each request, keep a Map of id to resolvers, look up the reply
questions.why: An id-keyed Map of pending `{ resolve, reject }` pairs is the standard RPC shape over any message channel (workers, WebSockets, iframes). FIFO matching breaks as soon as the worker finishes a short job before a long one, a worker per call wastes start-up time, and `postMessage` returns undefined.
questions.asked: This is the core of every worker helper library; drawing the Map of pending requests is what a strong answer does.

questions.q: What does `worker.terminate()` do to a task the worker is in the middle of?
choices: It pauses the worker, and `worker.resume()` continues where it stopped
It waits for the current message handler to finish, then stops the worker
It stops the worker straight away; the task is abandoned and sends no reply
It throws an AbortError inside the handler so the worker can clean up
questions.why: Terminate kills the worker thread immediately with no cleanup hook and no reply, so any caller waiting on a promise will hang unless your wrapper rejects pending requests itself. That makes it usable as a hard cancel for a runaway computation, which a signal cannot interrupt.
questions.asked: A good follow-up to 'how do you cancel CPU work': abort signals can't interrupt a busy loop, but terminating the worker can.

questions.q: Your app needs `SharedArrayBuffer` to share memory with a worker. In current browsers, what must the page do first?
choices: Nothing: it has been available unconditionally since browsers added it
Be served with COOP and COEP headers so the page is cross-origin isolated
Ask for the user's permission through the Permissions API at start-up
Load the worker with `{ type: "module" }` so memory sharing is enabled
questions.why: After Spectre, browsers only expose SharedArrayBuffer when `crossOriginIsolated` is true, which needs `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` (or credentialless). Those headers can break third-party embeds, which is why most apps copy or transfer data instead.
questions.asked: Rarely needed in CRUD apps, but knowing the header cost explains why teams choose transfer over sharing.

questions.q: What is the difference between a service worker and a dedicated Web Worker?
choices: A service worker sits between the page and the network and outlives the tab
A service worker can read the DOM, while a dedicated worker cannot
A dedicated worker is shared by all tabs, a service worker by only one
They are the same thing; "service worker" is the older name for it
questions.why: A service worker is an event-driven proxy for fetches, push and offline caching, registered per scope and started by the browser as needed. A dedicated worker is a background thread owned by one page for computation. Neither can touch the DOM.
questions.asked: Candidates often mix the two up; the answer should mention offline caching versus off-main-thread CPU work.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), roughly how long until this logs `[ 300, 300, 300 ]`?
choices: Immediately
About 600 ms
About 900 ms
About 300 ms
questions.why: The three timers start as soon as the array is built, so they run concurrently; `Array.fromAsync` just awaits each element in turn, and all three are done after about 300 ms. It only serialises work when the source is an async iterable that starts each step lazily.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand that promises start when created, not when awaited.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), roughly how long until this logs `[ 1, 2, 3 ]`?
choices: About 200 ms
About 100 ms
About 300 ms
Immediately
questions.why: An async generator does no work until someone asks for the next value, so `Array.fromAsync` drives it one page at a time: three sequential 100 ms waits. That laziness is what makes generators good for paging an API, and also why they are not a way to get concurrency.
questions.asked: Pairs well with the array version: the difference is when the work starts.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: It logs 'caught b' at 10 ms, before 'a'
The process crashes with an unhandled rejection 'b'
It logs 'a' and ignores the rejected promise
It logs 'a', then 'caught b'
questions.why: The second promise rejects at 10 ms while the loop is still awaiting the first, and nothing has attached a handler to it yet, so Node 24 treats it as unhandled and exits. Use `Promise.all`/`allSettled` for an array of already-started promises; `for await` suits lazy sources.
questions.asked: A real production crash pattern; strong candidates explain 'handled later' versus 'handled in time'.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: true TimeoutError
true AggregateError
true AbortError
false undefined
questions.why: `AbortSignal.any` aborts as soon as any input signal aborts, and takes that signal's reason, here the TimeoutError from `AbortSignal.timeout`. It is how you combine a user Cancel button with a deadline in one `signal` option.
questions.asked: Combining cancellation sources used to need hand-written listener plumbing; knowing the built-in is a current-knowledge check.

questions.q: Inside a long async job that receives a `signal`, what does `signal.throwIfAborted()` do?
choices: Waits until the signal aborts and then throws an AbortError
Registers the current function to be killed when the signal aborts
Aborts the signal immediately and throws its reason to the caller
Throws the signal's `reason` if it has already aborted, else does nothing
questions.why: It is a synchronous check point: call it between steps (each page, row batch or retry) so a cancelled job stops at the next boundary. JavaScript cannot interrupt running code from outside, so your own functions only stop where they check.
questions.asked: Shows you know cancellation in JS is cooperative, not pre-emptive.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: It throws: already aborted
page closed
user cancelled
undefined
questions.why: A signal aborts once. The second `abort()` is a no-op, so the reason stays the first one and abort listeners do not fire again. That makes it safe for several code paths (Cancel button, unmount, timeout) to call `abort()` on the same controller.
questions.asked: Checks you know abort is idempotent, which matters when cleanup code may run more than once.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: A TypeError: not a promise
then called, then 42
{ then: [Function: then] }
42 only
questions.why: `await` (like `Promise.resolve` and returning from a `.then`) adopts any object with a callable `then`, calling it with resolve and reject. That is how old promise libraries and query builders such as Knex interoperate with native promises, and why putting a `then` method on a plain object is a trap.
questions.asked: Explains why `await queryBuilder` runs a query, which confuses people new to ORMs and query builders.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: true
false, because q wraps p in a second layer
undefined
false, because a new promise is always created
questions.why: `Promise.resolve` returns its argument unchanged when it is already a native promise from the same constructor, so no wrapper is created. Promises also never nest: resolving with a promise adopts its state, so a `Promise<Promise<T>>` cannot exist.
questions.asked: A precise-model question; strong candidates add that promises flatten, so double wrapping is impossible.

questions.q: A config loader might throw synchronously or return a promise. What does `Promise.try(load)` (ES2025, Node 24) give you?
choices: It runs `load` on the next macrotask so it never blocks the caller
It swallows sync throws and resolves the promise with undefined instead
It retries `load` until it resolves or the retry limit is reached
A promise either way: a sync throw becomes a rejection you can `.catch`
questions.why: `Promise.try(fn)` calls `fn` immediately and turns a return value, a returned promise or a thrown error into one promise. Without it, a sync throw escapes before `.catch` is attached; the old workaround was `Promise.resolve().then(fn)`, which also delayed the call by a tick.
questions.asked: A current-knowledge check; the strong answer names the old `new Promise` or `.then` workaround it replaces.

questions.q: In Node 24, what happens when this ES module runs?
choices: It logs 'start' and hangs forever, keeping the process alive
It logs 'start' and 'end', because top-level await has a timeout
It logs 'start', warns about an unsettled top-level await, and exits with code 13
It throws a SyntaxError, because await needs an async function
questions.why: A promise that never settles doesn't keep the event loop alive on its own. When the loop empties with the module still waiting, Node prints 'Detected unsettled top-level await' and exits with code 13, which is the clue when a script mysteriously stops at an await.
questions.asked: A debugging question: exit code 13 is a lost resolve call, usually a callback that never fired.

questions.q: How do you turn an image load into a promise you can `await`?
choices: `img.onload = resolve(img); img.onerror = reject(img);`
`img.onload = () => resolve(img); img.onerror = reject;`
`return img.onload;` so the promise resolves when the image loads
`await img.load(); resolve(img);` inside the executor
questions.why: Wrap event-based APIs by calling resolve and reject from the success and failure handlers. The last option calls both functions immediately instead of passing them, so the promise resolves before the image has loaded, and returning from the executor is ignored.
questions.asked: 'Promisify this callback or event API' is a common live-coding warm-up.

questions.q: Fifty requests get 401 at the same moment because the access token expired. What should the refresh logic do?
choices: Share one in-flight refresh promise; all 50 await it, then retry once
Retry each request after a short delay until the token becomes valid again
Let each request refresh the token itself, since refresh endpoints are cheap
Set `refreshing = true`, and have the other requests fail if the flag is set
questions.why: Store the pending refresh promise and hand it to every caller, then clear it when it settles, so exactly one refresh happens. Fifty refreshes can invalidate each other if refresh tokens rotate, a boolean flag gives waiting callers nothing to wait on, and blind retries never get a token.
questions.asked: A common real-world auth bug; interviewers like hearing about rotating refresh tokens as the reason it matters.

questions.q: A user debounces a search input by 300 ms. Which problem does debouncing NOT solve?
choices: Wasting server capacity on queries the user never waited for
Firing requests for half-typed words such as "wid" in "widget"
Sending a request on every keystroke while the user is still typing
An older, slower response arriving after a newer one and overwriting it
questions.why: Debouncing only reduces how many requests start; two requests can still be in flight when the user pauses, types, and pauses again, and they may finish out of order. You still need to abort the previous request or ignore stale responses.
questions.asked: Many candidates stop at 'debounce it'; the strong answer adds cancellation or a request id.

questions.q: A payment POST times out on the client, and the retry creates a second charge. What stops this?
choices: Raising the client timeout so the first request always completes
Retrying POST only when the first attempt returned a 5xx status code
Sending an idempotency key the server uses to return the first result
Using PUT instead of POST, because PUT is always safe to retry
questions.why: A timeout tells you nothing about whether the server processed the request. An `Idempotency-Key` header generated once per user action lets the server recognise the repeat and replay the stored response. Longer timeouts only make the ambiguity rarer, and changing the verb does not change the server logic.
questions.asked: Any interview touching payments or orders gets here; the key point is that timeouts are ambiguous.

questions.q: Your API retries a failing dependency 3 times, and the service that calls you also retries 3 times. The dependency goes down. What happens to its load?
choices: It doubles, since two layers each add one more round of calls
It multiplies: each user call can become 16 calls to the dependency
It drops to zero, because callers back off as soon as it fails
It stays the same, because retries only happen after a failure
questions.why: Retries multiply across layers: 4 attempts from the caller, each triggering 4 attempts from you, is 16 calls per user action, just as the dependency is struggling. Retry at one layer only, and use retry budgets or a circuit breaker so failures shed load instead of adding it.
questions.asked: Retry amplification is how a small outage becomes a big one; mentioning where retries should live is the strong answer.

questions.q: In a browser tab, why might `await res.json()` on a 60 MB response freeze the UI even though it is awaited?
choices: The body downloads asynchronously, but the JSON parse itself runs on the main thread
fetch downloads large bodies synchronously once they pass 50 MB
The browser disables rendering while any fetch body is still open
Awaiting a large promise holds the event loop until it settles
questions.why: Only the network part is off-thread; building a huge object graph from JSON is CPU work on the main thread, so it becomes one long task. Paginate, stream NDJSON, or parse in a worker. Awaiting doesn't block anything by itself.
questions.asked: Tests the difference between asynchronous I/O and synchronous CPU work hiding behind an await.

questions.q: Two open tabs of your app must not both refresh the auth token at once. Which browser API coordinates them?
choices: A `Promise.race` between the two tabs’ refresh calls
A `setTimeout` offset per tab so the refreshes never overlap
A module-level `let refreshing` flag shared by both tabs
The Web Locks API: `navigator.locks.request('refresh', fn)`
questions.why: Each tab has its own JavaScript heap, so an in-memory flag or promise only dedupes within one tab. `navigator.locks.request` grants a named lock to one context at a time across same-origin tabs and workers, and releases it when your callback's promise settles.
questions.asked: Multi-tab races are a real source of logout bugs; knowing that each tab has its own heap is the key insight.

questions.q: After a user logs out in one tab, the other open tabs of your app should log out too. Which API is the simplest fit?
choices: A dedicated Web Worker, since all tabs share the same worker
Polling `document.hidden` every second to detect other tabs
A `BroadcastChannel` that every tab listens on for a logout message
A shared `Promise` exported from the auth module in every tab
questions.why: `new BroadcastChannel("auth")` delivers messages to every same-origin tab, iframe and worker that opened a channel with that name. Module state is per tab, and a dedicated worker belongs to one page (a SharedWorker could work, but is more machinery). The `storage` event on localStorage is the older alternative.
questions.asked: A practical multi-tab question; mentioning the older `storage` event trick shows breadth.

questions.q: Why is rejecting with a string, as in `reject("not found")`, a bad habit?
choices: Node 24 converts string rejections into a SyntaxError
A string carries no stack trace, name or cause, so the error is hard to trace
`Promise.all` ignores rejections whose reason is not an Error
Strings cannot be caught by `try/catch` around an `await`
questions.why: You can reject with any value and `catch` still receives it, but only an Error records where it was created and supports `name`, `cause` and `instanceof` checks. Code downstream that reads `err.message` also gets undefined. Lint rules such as `prefer-promise-reject-errors` enforce this.
questions.asked: A code-review staple; the strong answer mentions stack traces and consistent error handling.

questions.q: A save handler awaits `validate(order)`, then `reserveStock(order)`, then `charge(order)`, each using the previous result. Should you use `Promise.all`?
choices: No: the steps depend on each other, so sequential awaits are right
No, because `Promise.all` cannot run functions that take arguments
Yes, because running the three together is always faster
Yes, but only if each function also receives an AbortSignal
questions.why: Parallelise only independent work. These steps have a data and business dependency (never charge before stock is reserved), so running them together would be a bug. The mistake to avoid is the opposite case: sequentially awaiting calls that do not depend on each other.
questions.asked: Interviewers check you don't overcorrect after learning 'avoid sequential awaits'.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const values = await Promise.all([1, Promise.resolve(2), 'three']);
console.log(values);
choices: A TypeError: 1 is not a promise
[ undefined, 2, undefined ]
questions.why: Every element goes through `Promise.resolve`, so plain values pass straight through and the result keeps input order. That lets you mix cached values and pending requests in one call.
questions.asked: A quick check of what the combinators accept; useful when some values are cached and some are fetched.

questions.q: Your page memoises requests in `cache.set(url, fetch(url).then((r) => r.json()))`. The server is down for a minute. What goes wrong afterwards?
choices: Each call blocks until the server comes back, then all resolve
Nothing: the next call retries because rejected promises expire
The rejected promise stays cached, so every later call fails instantly
The cache fills with duplicate promises for the same URL
questions.why: A cached promise keeps whatever state it settled in, so a failure is cached forever. Delete the entry in a `.catch` (and rethrow), or cache only fulfilled values, so the next call tries again.
questions.asked: Promise caching is a common optimisation; forgetting to evict failures is the classic bug that follows it.

questions.q: An API allows 10 requests per second. You run your calls through a pool with a concurrency limit of 10. Are you within the rate limit?
choices: Yes, because at most 10 requests are ever in flight together
Only if each request takes at least a second; fast ones exceed it
Yes, because the pool waits a second between each batch of 10
No, because a pool always sends all requests at the start
questions.why: A concurrency limit caps how many run at once, not how many start per second: with 100 ms responses a pool of 10 sends about 100 per second. A rate limit needs a token bucket or a scheduled start time, often combined with a concurrency cap.
questions.asked: Mixing up 'in flight' and 'per second' is common; the strong answer names a token bucket.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: 1 number, then 2 number
Promise object, then 2 number
Promise object, then Promise object
1 number only
questions.why: Inside an async generator, `yield` awaits a promise before handing the value out, so consumers never see a raw promise. A sync generator used with `for await` would also unwrap it, but plain `for...of` over a sync generator would give you the promise itself.
questions.asked: Checks the precise rules of async generators, which matters when you write paging helpers.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: SyntaxError
Promise { { a: 1 } }
TypeError
questions.why: `await` binds more loosely than the member call, so this runs `fetch(...).json()` on the promise, which has no `json` method: TypeError. Write `await (await fetch(url)).json()`, or better, two lines with a `res.ok` check in between.
questions.asked: A very common first-week bug; the two-line version with an `ok` check is what reviewers want to see.

questions.q: Node's `fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { ... })` uses an error-first callback. What does that convention mean?
choices: The callback runs only on failure; success returns the data
The callback is called before the file is read, then again after
The first argument is an error or null; results come after it
Errors are thrown synchronously, and the callback gets only data
questions.why: Node callbacks take `(err, ...results)`: check `err` first, and only use the results when it is null. Throwing inside such a callback does not reach a surrounding `try/catch`, which is one reason promise-based APIs (`fs/promises`) replaced them.
questions.asked: Older codebases and libraries still use this style, and wrapping it in a promise is a common task.

questions.q: A dashboard view starts `setInterval(refresh, 5000)` when it opens. Users navigate between views all day. What goes wrong?
choices: The browser merges identical intervals, so refresh runs once
Each visit adds another interval, so refreshes pile up and leak
The interval throws once its view is removed from the page
Nothing: intervals stop automatically when the view is hidden
questions.why: An interval runs until `clearInterval` is called with its id, whatever happens to the DOM. Each visit adds one more, so requests multiply and the callbacks keep old views in memory. Clear it in the teardown path (a React effect cleanup, for example).
questions.asked: Checks that you own cleanup for everything you start: timers, listeners and requests.

questions.q: In an old CommonJS script without top-level await, why do people write `(async () => { ... })()`?
choices: It lets them use `await` inside it, since only async functions allow it
It stops the process from exiting until every promise has settled
It turns any errors inside into warnings instead of crashes
It makes the whole file run on a background thread
questions.why: An async IIFE is a quick way to get an async function body at the top level of a CommonJS file. It returns a promise, so add `.catch(...)` to it, or a rejection inside becomes an unhandled rejection. ES modules can just use top-level await.
questions.asked: Common in scripts and older Node code; strong candidates mention the missing `.catch`.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: [ 'a', undefined, 'c' ]
It throws Error: b
questions.why: Each settled result is `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`, and `allSettled` itself never rejects. Filtering on `status` is the standard way to keep the successes and report the failures separately.
questions.asked: Bulk operations with partial failure are routine CRUD work, so the result shape is worth knowing cold.

questions.q: A page awaits `Promise.all([getUser(), getOrders()])`, and the orders service never responds. What does the user see?
choices: The user data renders, and orders show an error after 30 s
An error, because `Promise.all` rejects promises that take too long
The page waits forever, since one pending promise holds up `all`
The user data renders at once, and orders render as undefined
questions.why: `Promise.all` settles only when every input has fulfilled or one has rejected, and a hung request does neither. Give each call a timeout (`AbortSignal.timeout`), and consider rendering the parts independently so one slow service does not block the page.
questions.asked: Leads naturally into timeouts and partial rendering, which is what interviewers want to discuss.

questions.q: Inside a dedicated worker script, how do you send the finished result back to the page?
choices: `return result` from the `onmessage` handler
`self.postMessage(result)`
`window.postMessage(result)`
`document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("done"))`
questions.why: In a worker the global is `self` (a DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope), and `self.postMessage` fires a `message` event on the Worker object in the page. Return values from handlers are ignored, and there is no `window` or `document` in a worker.
questions.asked: The absolute basics of the worker API, often asked before a worker design question.

questions.q: What does `new Worker(new URL('./parse.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })` let the worker script do?
choices: Use `import`/`export`, so it can import your shared modules
Read and update the DOM through an imported `document`
Run on the main thread, like any other module script
Share variables with the page through ES module imports
questions.why: A module worker loads its script as an ES module, so it can `import` your parsing code instead of using `importScripts`. It still gets its own separate copy of every module, with no shared state or DOM. Bundlers such as Vite recognise this `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` pattern.
questions.asked: Module workers are the modern default; knowing the bundler-friendly URL pattern shows hands-on use.

questions.q: In Node 24, what does this log?
questions.code: setTimeout((greeting, name) => console.log(greeting + ', ' + name), 10, 'Hi', 'Ada');
choices: Nothing: the extra arguments are an error
10, Hi
undefined, undefined
Hi, Ada
questions.why: Arguments after the delay are passed to the callback when it runs. It is an alternative to wrapping the call in an arrow function, which most people use instead because it reads more clearly.
questions.asked: A small API detail that shows up in code reviews of older code.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), roughly how long does this take?
choices: About 200 ms
Immediately
About 600 ms
About 400 ms
questions.why: An `await` inside `for...of` pauses the loop until each save finishes, so the three run one after another: about 600 ms. That is the right shape when order matters or the server must not be flooded; use `Promise.all` when the saves are independent.
questions.asked: Pairs with the forEach trap; the strong answer says when sequential is actually what you want.

questions.q: Which async/await version behaves the same as this chain?
choices: `async function load(id) { try { const u = getUser(id); return await getTeam(u.teamId); } catch { return null; } }`
`async function load(id) { try { const u = await getUser(id); return await getTeam(u.teamId); } catch { return null; } }`
`async function load(id) { try { const u = await getUser(id); return getTeam(u.teamId); } catch { return null; } }`
`async function load(id) { const u = await getUser(id); try { return await getTeam(u.teamId); } catch { return null; } }`
questions.why: The `.catch` covers failures from both calls. Without `return await`, a rejection from `getTeam` skips the catch; putting only the second call in the try misses `getUser` failures; and dropping the first `await` reads `teamId` off a promise.
questions.asked: Refactoring `.then` chains to async/await is routine, and this is where it quietly changes behaviour.

questions.q: What does `await` pause?
choices: Only the current async function; other code keeps running
Every async function in the module, until the promise settles
Nothing: it only marks where a promise may be returned
The whole JavaScript thread, until the promise settles
questions.why: At an `await`, the async function returns control to its caller, and the rest of the function is scheduled to resume when the promise settles. Meanwhile the event loop runs other tasks, clicks and requests. This is why one slow request does not freeze the page.
questions.asked: A foundational check; 'it waits' is vague, 'it suspends this function and yields to the event loop' is the answer.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: A Timeout object
undefined
woke
questions.why: Node's `timers/promises` version of setTimeout returns a promise that resolves with the optional value after the delay, and accepts `{ signal }` for cancellation. It replaces hand-written `sleep` helpers in Node code.
questions.asked: Shows familiarity with the promise-based Node APIs rather than wrapping everything by hand.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
questions.code:
const signal = AbortSignal.abort();
console.log(signal.aborted, signal.reason.name);
choices: false AbortError
false undefined
true AbortError
true TimeoutError
questions.why: `AbortSignal.abort(reason?)` returns a signal that is already aborted, with a default AbortError reason. It is handy in tests, and for making a function bail out when its caller has already given up.
questions.asked: Useful for testing cancellation paths without timers.

questions.q: What is wrong with this save handler?
choices: Nothing: `api.save` blocks until the request completes
The toast shows before the request has finished or even failed
`setSaving(false)` throws because the request is still running
The request is cancelled as soon as `onSave` returns
questions.why: `api.save` returns a promise immediately, so the spinner flips off and 'Saved' appears before the server answers, and a failure becomes an unhandled rejection. Make the handler async, `await` the save in try/catch, and clear the flag in `finally`.
questions.asked: Missing awaits in UI handlers are a top code-review finding.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what order do these log in?
choices: listener, after dispatch
after dispatch only
It depends on the event loop phase
after dispatch, listener
questions.why: `dispatchEvent` (like Node's `emitter.emit`) calls listeners synchronously, one after another, before it returns. Events are not queued as tasks, so a slow listener blocks the code that dispatched the event.
questions.asked: Many assume events are asynchronous; knowing they aren't explains a whole class of ordering bugs.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: It logs [ Promise { true } ]
It logs [ 3 ]
It logs []
It logs [ 1, 2, 3 ]
questions.why: `filter` does not await: every callback returns a promise, and any promise object is truthy, so nothing is removed. Resolve the checks first (`await Promise.all(ids.map(isActive))`), then filter by index.
questions.asked: The filter version of the forEach trap, and a likely follow-up when you answer that one well.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: It throws a TypeError
true true
true false
false false
questions.why: Structured clone tracks objects it has already copied, so cycles and shared references are preserved in the copy. `JSON.stringify` throws 'Converting circular structure to JSON' on the same object.
questions.asked: Rounds out the structuredClone versus JSON comparison with cycles.

questions.q: You build a pool of image-processing workers in the browser. What is a sensible pool size?
choices: One worker per image, so every image is processed at the same time
About `navigator.hardwareConcurrency - 1`, leaving a core for the page
Exactly one, because the browser only runs one worker at a time
A fixed 64, since idle workers cost nothing to keep around
questions.why: CPU-bound work cannot go faster than the cores you have, and each worker costs start-up time and memory. Size the pool near the core count (leaving room for the main thread) and queue the jobs.
questions.asked: Links worker pools to concurrency limits, which interviewers like to see connected.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?
choices: It rejects: chunks must be bytes
It logs '' because the stream is locked
It logs 'abc' once the stream ends
It logs 'a,b,c', joined by commas
questions.why: A Response body must be a stream of bytes. Pipe string chunks through `new TextEncoderStream()` first, and then `.text()` gives you back "abc". Wrapping a stream in `new Response` is a handy way to collect it, as long as it carries bytes.
questions.asked: Shows you know the text-versus-bytes boundary in web streams, which is where most stream bugs live.

questions.q: An import of 200 rows ends with 12 failures from `Promise.allSettled`. What is the best next step for the retry?
choices: Treat all 200 as failed and roll back the saved ones by hand
Retry the rejected rows at once with no delay, until all succeed
Re-run the whole import, since partial results are unreliable
Retry only the rejected rows, keeping their index to report them
questions.why: `allSettled` preserves input order, so each rejected result's index identifies the row. Retry just those with backoff and a cap, and report the ones that still fail; re-running everything duplicates writes unless the saves are idempotent.
questions.asked: Partial failure handling is where bulk features go wrong in production.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what does this log?
choices: undefined
'ok' after an unhandled rejection warning
ok
It throws Error: db down
questions.why: A `return` in `finally` overrides the pending throw, so the error vanishes and the promise fulfils with 'ok'. Keep `finally` for cleanup only; ESLint's `no-unsafe-finally` flags this.

questions.q: In Node 24 (ES module), what happens?

It logs 'after', then crashes with an uncaught Error: micro
It logs 'after', then an unhandled rejection warning
It logs 'caught', then 'after'

questions.q: In Node 24, what does this print?
questions.code:
setTimeout(() => console.log('reminder'), 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
setTimeout(() => console.log('tick'), 50);
choices: A TimeoutOverflowWarning, then 'reminder' at once and 'tick'
'tick', then a RangeError for the oversized delay
'tick' only, as the long timer is silently dropped
'tick' after 50 ms, then 'reminder' 30 days later
questions.why: Delays are stored as signed 32-bit milliseconds (about 24.8 days); anything larger is treated as 1 ms, and Node warns. Browsers do the same without a warning. Schedule far-future work in a job scheduler or database, not a timer.
questions.asked: A real production bug in reminder and subscription features; the fix is persistence, not a bigger timer.

questions.q: An API handler has a 2-second budget and calls three services in sequence. How should the timeouts on those calls be set?
choices: A fixed 500 ms each, whatever the earlier calls used up
Two seconds each, so every call gets the full budget
No timeouts, and let the load balancer cut the request off
From one deadline: each call gets the time that remains
questions.why: Per-call timeouts that ignore the others can add up to 6 s, long after the client gave up. Compute a deadline once and pass the remainder along (for example `AbortSignal.timeout(deadline - Date.now())`), so work stops when nobody is waiting.
questions.asked: Deadline propagation separates people who have debugged slow cascading requests from those who have not.

questions.q: A test checks that `loadUser(-1)` rejects. Why does it pass even when `loadUser` resolves?
choices: The test runner treats any returned promise as a pass
`.rejects` only works with Jest, not with Vitest
The assertion is never awaited, so the test ends before it runs
`toThrow` cannot match messages on rejected promises
questions.why: The `.rejects` assertion is itself a promise. Without `await` (or `return`), the test finishes synchronously and passes, and the later assertion failure is lost or reported against another test. Write `await expect(...).rejects.toThrow(...)`.
questions.asked: False-passing async tests are common; spotting the missing await is a quick signal of test experience.

questions.q: Your worker posts 'progress 10%', 'progress 20%' and then 'done' with three `postMessage` calls. In what order does the page receive them?
choices: In any order, since each message travels separately
In the order sent, one 'message' event each
Only 'done', because later messages replace earlier ones
All three merged into a single event with an array
questions.why: Messages on one channel are delivered in the order they were posted, each as its own event. Delivery is asynchronous though: they arrive as tasks on the page's event loop, so a busy main thread delays them.
questions.asked: Progress reporting from workers relies on this guarantee.

questions.q: A worker computes a report for a filter the user has since changed. How do you stop the stale result from being shown?
choices: Tag each job with an id and ignore replies for any old id
Call `postMessage` again with the new filter; the old job is replaced
Wrap the call in `Promise.race` so the older reply is rejected
Pass an AbortSignal in `postMessage` so the worker stops at once
questions.why: A busy worker can't process a cancel message until its current job ends, and signals can't be posted. Ignore stale replies by job id (or terminate and recreate the worker for long jobs). Posting again only queues a second job.
questions.asked: The worker version of the search race; the strong answer weighs ignoring against terminating.

questions.q: You call an async function without `await` on purpose: `sendAnalytics(event)`. What should you add?
choices: A `setTimeout` wrapper so it runs after the current request
`await` anyway, because unawaited calls are cancelled
Nothing: a promise nobody awaits cannot reject
A `.catch` that logs, so a failure is not an unhandled rejection
questions.why: Fire-and-forget is fine for non-critical work, but a rejection with no handler crashes Node 24 and pollutes the browser console. Attach `.catch(log)` (or `void` it after handling) so the floating promise is deliberate, which also satisfies `no-floating-promises`.
questions.asked: Checks you can tell deliberate fire-and-forget from a forgotten await.

AbortError

questions.asked: The building block of every cancellable helper you write yourself.

questions.q: Why is `for await (const row of rows)` over a plain array of already-resolved values not an error?
questions.code: for await (const n of [1, 2, 3]) console.log(n);
choices: It is an error: `for await` needs an async iterable
`for await` falls back to the sync iterator and awaits each value
The array is converted into a ReadableStream behind the scenes
It only works because the values are numbers, not objects
questions.why: When there is no `Symbol.asyncIterator`, `for await` uses `Symbol.iterator` and awaits each value, so it logs 1, 2, 3. That is convenient, but it also means `for await` over an array of pending promises has the unhandled-rejection trap.
questions.asked: Fills in the precise rule behind for-await, which explains both its convenience and its trap.
